evidence.snippet: Physiotherapy and non-surgical treatment including splinting led to an improvement of his contractures, increased range of motion, and improved muscular tone in his lower limbs.
evidence.explanation: The Family 3 survivor improved with physiotherapy and splinting; this directly corrects the prior claim that contractures cannot improve.

treatments/3.description: Physiotherapy and splinting improved contractures, range of motion and lower-limb tone in one GLDN survivor. Other survivors underwent selected orthopedic procedures. These observed courses do not establish a uniform protocol or irreversible contracture trajectory.

evidence.snippet: Perinatal palliative care is principled to support families through this uncertainty using shared decision-making to establish goals of care.
evidence.explanation: This is the authors’ care principle for uncertain LCCS2 outcomes, not a measured treatment effect or a recommendation to withhold intensive care.

evidence.snippet: She had consultations with pediatric urology and a Perinatal Palliative Care Team including representatives from neonatology, pediatrics, Chaplaincy, among others. Given the family’s previous experience and the counseled expectations for infants born with LCCS2, patient requested a supported comfort care model of care after birth.
evidence.explanation: The mother carrying the second affected sibling received multidisciplinary consultation and initially chose supported comfort care. This is an observed family decision, separate from the authors’ general principle.

evidence.snippet: Despite expectations to allow a natural death after birth, she continued to have respiratory drive and live. The family’s goals of care pivoted to accept neonatal intensive level care with perceived non-aggressive interventions such as nasal cannula oxygen support, enteral feedings via nasogastric tube, thermoregulation support, and Foley catheter.
evidence.explanation: The second sibling’s continued respiratory drive changed the family’s goals. These actual noninvasive respiratory, nutritional and supportive interventions demonstrate that the care plan was revisable; they do not prove efficacy or a uniform survival trajectory.

treatments/4.description: Multidisciplinary perinatal palliative care supported a family with prenatal ERBB3-associated LCCS2. The family initially requested supported comfort care, then accepted nasal oxygen, nasogastric feeding, thermoregulation and bladder catheterization when the infant continued to breathe. Shared goals can change with the observed course; palliative care does not imply comfort-only care or an identical prognosis across LCCS subtypes.

evidence.snippet: Due to persistent respiratory insufficiency, inability to cough, and insufficient swallowing, he underwent tracheostomy at 6 weeks of age. His respiratory function gradually improved, and he was successfully weaned from ventilatory support at nine months of age and subsequently decannulated at 19 months of age.
evidence.explanation: This is the Family 3 survivor’s indication and subsequent course, not evidence that tracheostomy caused recovery or that decannulation is expected in every child.

treatments/5.description: Tracheostomy provided access for respiratory support in selected GLDN-associated survivors with persistent respiratory insufficiency. The Family 3 child underwent the procedure at six weeks for respiratory insufficiency, ineffective cough and swallowing difficulty, then weaned from ventilation at nine months and was decannulated at 19 months. Other children remained dependent; the procedure does not itself reverse pulmonary hypoplasia or neuromuscular weakness.

evidence.snippet: He underwent surgical treatment for bilateral hip luxation and clubfeet (age 2 years) and scoliosis with Harrington rod insertion (age 9 years).
evidence.explanation: The Family 2 survivor had these specific operations at distinct ages. Later mobility and respiratory changes occurred during a broader course of care and are not attributed solely to surgery.

treatments/6.description: A GLDN-associated Family 2 survivor underwent operations for bilateral hip luxation and clubfeet at two years and scoliosis instrumentation at nine years. These procedures addressed selected structural problems alongside respiratory, nutritional and rehabilitation care; the case does not isolate a surgical benefit or establish a standard operative plan for LCCS.

evidence.snippet: Our data corroborate those of other reports, demonstrating that LCCS11 is not universally lethal, but long-term survivors are at risk of progressive neuromuscular compromise.
evidence.explanation: The newer founder series independently supports variable lethality and later morbidity.

open_questions/0.rationale: Published GLDN series include terminations, neonatal deaths and long survivors, with differing denominators and support. The 2025 founder report includes four early deaths and one survivor with later progressive compromise. These data establish variable outcome but do not separate residual function, modifiers and care effects.

evidence.snippet: Genotype-phenotype correlation in these patients and previously published cases with respective variants resulted in the definition of a DST-associated lethal congenital contracture syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Establishes DST as the gene defining a lethal congenital contracture syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Variants that also impact DST-a besides DST-b result in a more severe, lethal congenital contracture syndrome.
evidence.explanation: Gives the isoform-dependent severity relationship that separates the lethal phenotype from the congenital myopathy.

open_questions/1.rationale: The source establishes causal combined-isoform involvement, now represented by a qualified edge to contractures. It does not identify the relative neuronal and muscle mechanisms in the lethal cases; the separate DST-b-only cohort is not evidence of their biopsy or cardiac phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We report two Irish Traveller families with a previously undescribed lethal skeletal dysplasia characterized by fetal akinesia, shortening of all long bones, multiple contractures, rib anomalies, thoracic dysplasia, pulmonary hypoplasia and protruding abdomen.
evidence.explanation: The original lethal skeletal-dysplasia families establish the LCCS10 clinical scope; the later APUG-like neonates are not used as its denominator.

open_questions/2.rationale: The original lethal families had akinesia and skeletal dysplasia, and their fibroblasts had both mitotic and ciliary abnormalities. Qualified causal links are represented. The unresolved issue is tissue and process attribution, not whether the causal genotype or the fetal movement phenotype exists. Surviving APUG-like cases are not used to supply LCCS10 visceral findings.

evidence.snippet: Homozygous gldn−/− mice do not have apparent neurologic deficits or features of arthrogryposis and demonstrate normal nerve conduction and peripheral nervous system myelin (Feinberg, et al., 2010).
evidence.explanation: The primary clinical paper summarizes the null-mouse contrast; this is model-organism evidence, not a negative finding in human GLDN disease.

evidence.snippet: Nerve conduction velocity studies performed at 1 week of age demonstrated axonal motor and sensory neuropathy but were normal when repeated at 7 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Human longitudinal variability is another constraint on a permanent, uniform conduction-block model.

open_questions/3.rationale: Human nerve abnormalities support the nodopathy mechanism, but preserved conduction and absence of arthrogryposis in null mice constrain a simple universal loss-of-function-to-complete-conduction-block model. Allele, species and compensatory nodal mechanisms remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Sonography examination revealed hydrothorax, subcutaneous generalized edema, short long bones, fixed limb joints, absent fetal movements, fetal growth restriction (estimated fetal weight in the 4th percentile and absent end-diastolic flow in both umbilical arteries), and polyhydramnios (amniotic fluid index 28 cm) (Figure 1).
evidence.explanation: The coexisting flow abnormality constrains attribution of growth restriction solely to the fetal motor disorder.

open_questions/4.rationale: The rat paralysis experiment supports a qualified akinesia-to-growth-restriction contribution, now represented in the graph. It does not resolve the relative contribution in the GLDN-associated fetus with abnormal umbilical-artery flow. The reviewed LCCS sources establish hydrops but do not identify a subtype-specific fluid-balance mechanism; its absence in original ERBB3 and PIP5K1C kindreds constrains an obligatory consequence of contractures.

evidence.snippet: The pregnancy was terminated and postmortem studies confirmed the prenatal findings: distal arthrogryposis, fetal growth restriction, pulmonary hypoplasia, and retrognathia.
evidence.explanation: The primary case supports jaw retrusion, not mandibular size.

open_questions/5.rationale: Fetal immobility is a supported general deformation mechanism, with micrognathia and pterygia routes represented separately. The reviewed sources do not specifically resolve jaw retrusion or hip dislocation in the cited LCCS patients. A small mandible is not equivalent to retrusion, and local mechanical versus primary developmental attribution remains uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Individual LD_0333.0 was a girl with severe hypotonia and respiratory insufficiency that required a tracheostomy after birth, hypomyelinating neuropathy, bilateral hearing loss, bilateral optic nerve atrophy, lethargy, and neurogenic bladder.
evidence.explanation: Documents neurogenic bladder in a CNTNAP1-associated child, extending the subtype scope without identifying the responsible autonomic pathway.

open_questions/6.rationale: Human reports establish neurogenic bladder in both subtypes but do not localize the responsible autonomic lesion. Somatic anterior-horn loss alone does not establish the bladder mechanism; CNTNAP1 disease includes both central and peripheral pathology.

evidence.snippet: Insufficient swallowing aggravated by paresis of both the right vocal cord and right side of the soft palate prompted gastrostomy tube placement at 4 months of age.
evidence.explanation: Documents vocal cord paresis and its contribution to the swallowing failure.

evidence.snippet: Laryngoscopy demonstrated laryngo- and tracheomalacia, floppy epiglottis, and pooling of oral secretions.
evidence.explanation: The laryngoscopic findings explicitly establish laryngomalacia in this child.

open_questions/7.rationale: The source establishes focal paresis, diaphragm paralysis and laryngoscopic malacia in different children. Their downstream swallowing and respiratory contributions are represented where directly supported. It does not localize the upstream cause of paresis or establish that structural airway malacia is a direct consequence of gliomedin deficiency. Polysomnographic central apnea is separately reported; its coexistence with tracheomalacia does not establish an obstructive mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Motor and language development was delayed; he was able to sit independently at age 13 months and started to crawl at age 24 months.
evidence.explanation: The exact ages establish motor delay in the Family 3 survivor, without inferring cognitive impairment.

open_questions/8.rationale: The source documents delayed milestones and subsequent gains with growth and care. It does not separate peripheral motor dysfunction from mechanical restriction, prolonged illness or developmental contributors sufficiently to assign a specific causal edge to motor delay.

evidence.snippet: Individual LD_0158.0 is an 8 year old male with hypotonia and respiratory failure requiring intubation at birth and subsequent tracheotomy-dependency, congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy with arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, cleft palate, cortical vision loss, bilateral hearing loss, and neurogenic bladder.
evidence.explanation: This patient-level clinical observation establishes the findings but does not establish a single causal route for them.

open_questions/9.rationale: Central and peripheral glial-axonal disease provides plausible context, but the report does not connect the observed cortical visual loss, hearing loss, optic atrophy or palatal malformation to a specific demonstrated mechanism. Hearing-loss localization and the developmental cause of cleft palate remain unresolved; the established central hypomyelination and atrophy routes are represented separately.

evidence.snippet: AFB3 and AFB4 had pulmonary hypertension and a patent ductus arteriosus; whether these features were primary or secondary to respiratory insufficiency could not be determined.
evidence.explanation: The authors state the causal attribution limit for these two cardiopulmonary observations.

open_questions/10.rationale: The source explicitly states that primary versus secondary attribution could not be determined. The general developmental endocytosis hypothesis does not resolve this specific uncertainty, so no direct respiratory or genetic-mechanism edge is asserted.

evidence.snippet: He underwent surgical treatment for bilateral hip luxation and clubfeet (age 2 years) and scoliosis with Harrington rod insertion (age 9 years).
evidence.explanation: The GLDN Family 2 survivor underwent scoliosis surgery with Harrington rod insertion at age nine years. The hip procedure in the same sentence occurred at age two.

open_questions/11.rationale: The clinical course establishes scoliosis requiring surgery at age nine, alongside weakness, atrophy and congenital contractures. It does not identify the cause or provide serial spinal development sufficient to distinguish neuromuscular deformation from another developmental process. The surgery documents the phenotype, not a demonstrated causal intermediary.

evidence.snippet: Here we demonstrate that the primary defect in LAD is in the beta subunit gene.
evidence.explanation: Assigns the primary lesion to the shared beta subunit gene rather than to any individual alpha chain.

evidence.snippet: We identified five distinct beta subunit phenotypes in LAD patients: undetectable beta subunit mRNA and protein precursor; low levels of beta subunit mRNA and precursor; an aberrantly large beta subunit precursor, probably due to an extra glycosylation site; an aberrantly small precursor; and a grossly normal precursor.
evidence.explanation: The allelic heterogeneity that underlies the severe-versus-moderate split curated below, including the case where protein is made but does not work.

steps/1.description: Both copies of ITGB2 at 21q22.3 carry variants that abolish or cripple CD18. The original molecular study resolved five distinct beta-subunit phenotypes across patients - absent mRNA and precursor, low mRNA and precursor, an aberrantly large precursor, an aberrantly small precursor, and a grossly normal precursor - which is why surface expression ranges from undetectable to near-normal-but-nonfunctional. Most missense variants cluster in the conserved betaI domain encoded by exons 5-9, the ligand-binding face of the receptor.

evidence.snippet: Since the β and α subunits pair intracellularly, a decreased or mutated β subunit also leads to a decreased expression of the α subunit at the cell surface.
evidence.explanation: The intracellular-pairing requirement that makes a beta-chain defect take all four alpha chains down with it.

evidence.snippet: Decreased expression of the common β2 subunit leads to a similar decrease in the expression of all four α subunits on the leukocyte surface.
evidence.explanation: Confirms the loss spans all four alpha subunits rather than being restricted to LFA-1.

evidence.snippet: These include Mac-1 (complement receptor type 3), lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1), and p150,95.
evidence.explanation: Names the receptor family lost, from the classic clinical-molecular description of the disease.

steps/2.description: CD18 is the common beta chain of four heterodimers - LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18), Mac-1 (CD11b/CD18), p150,95 (CD11c/CD18) and CD11d/CD18. The alpha and beta subunits pair inside the cell before trafficking to the surface, so when the beta chain is absent or malformed the alpha chains cannot reach the membrane either. One gene defect therefore removes a whole receptor family, which is why the phenotype is broader than any single-integrin knockout would predict.

evidence.snippet: This deficiency leads to severe impairment of leukocyte adhesion to the vascular wall and leukocyte migration to sites of infection and inflammation.
evidence.explanation: The adhesion defect at the vessel wall, stated for CD18 deficiency directly.

evidence.snippet: Since VLA-4 is mainly expressed on monocytes and T cells, but not on neutrophils, it is not able to compensate for the loss of β2 integrins in LAD I
evidence.explanation: Explains why the neutrophil has no redundant arrest mechanism, which is why this node is absolute rather than partial in the neutrophil lineage.

steps/3.description: Selectin-mediated rolling is intact in LAD1 - the selectins and their ligands are untouched - but the neutrophil cannot convert rolling into integrin-mediated firm arrest on the inflamed vessel wall. LFA-1 binding to endothelial ICAM-1 and ICAM-2 is the step that fails. No other adhesion system substitutes: VLA-4, which lets monocytes and T cells arrest through a beta-1 route, is not expressed on neutrophils, so the neutrophil has no fallback.

evidence.snippet: The infiltrate comprised primarily lymphocytes, whereas neutrophils were confined within vessels.
evidence.explanation: Direct histological demonstration in patient tissue that neutrophils do not cross the vessel wall, which is the node's claim.

steps/4.description: Neutrophils remain confined within the vessel lumen and do not cross into infected or inflamed tissue. Histology of LAD1 lesions makes the point plainly - the inflammatory infiltrate is dense but composed of lymphocytes, with neutrophils visible inside vessels and absent from the tissue around them.

evidence.snippet: characterized by recurrent bacterial infections, impaired pus formation and wound healing
evidence.explanation: Names impaired wound healing as a defining feature of the disease.

evidence.snippet: The patients suffer from recurrent, life-threatening bacterial and fungal infections and from impaired wound healing.
evidence.explanation: Independent statement of the wound-healing defect alongside the infection phenotype.

steps/5.description: Wounds fail to repair and skin ulcers persist, because the neutrophil influx that initiates the repair programme does not occur. Clinically this appears as non-healing lesions that progress through repeated antibiotic courses and surgical debridement, and it is one of the features that resolves when the adhesion defect is corrected.

evidence.snippet: Characteristic features are delayed separation of the umbilical cord and strong leukocytosis, especially neutrophilia, during periods of infection.
evidence.explanation: The blood side of the inversion, described as characteristic of the disease.

evidence.snippet: IL-17-induced granulopoiesis factors and chemokines were readily detected in blood plasma of LAD-I patients
evidence.explanation: Ties the circulating neutrophilia to sustained granulopoietic drive rather than to a marrow abnormality, which is why the two compartments diverge.

steps/6.description: The signature inversion of this disease. Granulopoiesis is normal and unrestrained, so the circulating neutrophil count is high - markedly so during infection - while the tissue compartment behaves as if the patient were neutropenic. Every downstream consequence of the disease flows from this dissociation, and it is also why the blood count is actively misleading at the bedside: the one number a clinician reaches for moves in the opposite direction to the deficit.

evidence.snippet: Defective neutrophil recruitment in LAD-I patients or in LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18)-deficient mice--which exhibit the LAD-I periodontal phenotype--was associated with excessive production of predominantly T cell-derived IL-17 in the periodontal tissue
evidence.explanation: The human observation of excess T-cell-derived IL-17 in LAD-I periodontal tissue, and its attribution to the recruitment defect.

evidence.snippet: These data reveal that the elevated expression of IL-17 in LAD-I is compartmentalized rather than systemic.
evidence.explanation: The compartmentalisation, which is why this node is tagged TISSUE and not ORGANISM.

evidence.snippet: The phagocytosis of apoptotic neutrophils (efferocytosis) by tissue macrophages acts as a signal to down-regulate the production of interleukin-23 and therefore the downstream cytokines interleukin-17 and granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF).
evidence.explanation: States the feedback circuit whose input is missing here, which is the mechanism this node asserts.

steps/7.description: Tissue macrophages normally down-regulate IL-23 production when they phagocytose transmigrated apoptotic neutrophils. In LAD1 those neutrophils never arrive, so the brake is never applied and an otherwise physiological IL-23 response to the local microbiome runs unchecked, driving T-cell-derived IL-17 to high levels at the gingiva and skin. The elevation is compartmentalised rather than systemic - plasma IL-17 and IL-23 are low or absent - which matters because it means this is a local immunopathology, not a circulating inflammatory syndrome.

evidence.snippet: Affected individuals display neutrophilia, suffer from recurrent infections, and invariably develop early-onset generalized aggressive periodontitis featuring severe bone loss and premature loss of primary and permanent teeth
evidence.explanation: States the periodontal phenotype and its invariability in this disease.

evidence.snippet: quantification of bacterial counts in gingival tissue sections from LAD-I patients and healthy controls, using real-time PCR of the 16S rRNA gene, revealed that the bacterial load within the tissue of LAD-I patients was comparable to (if not less than) that of healthy controls
evidence.explanation: The measurement that refutes the tissue-invasive-infection reading of this phenotype, and so supports curating it as an immunopathology.

evidence.snippet: We observed progressive periodontal disease in all patients evaluated, despite prophylactic antibiotic use since infancy and access to dental care.
evidence.explanation: The clinical refractoriness to antimicrobial and mechanical management, which is the practical consequence of the mechanism.

steps/8.description: Early-onset, generalised, severe periodontitis with destruction of tooth-supporting connective tissue and alveolar bone, ending in loss of both primary and permanent dentition. Historically read as unpoliced periodontal infection, but the evidence does not support that: bacterial load within the diseased gingival tissue is comparable to or lower than in healthy controls, and the disease is refractory to antibiotics and to mechanical biofilm removal. The severity scales inversely with residual CD18, tying the dental phenotype quantitatively to the molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: characterized by recurrent bacterial infections, impaired pus formation and wound healing
evidence.explanation: The classic description, which names impaired pus formation alongside the infections rather than as an afterthought.

evidence.snippet: Children can also present with severe/recurrent bacterial or fungal infections, recalcitrant periodontitis, and/or necrotic skin wounds/lesions absent pus formation.
evidence.explanation: Contemporary consensus statement of the same presentation, and the source for including fungal infection rather than bacterial alone.

evidence.snippet: Chronic necrotic skin lesions, often incorrectly described as pyoderma gangrenosum (biopsy samples characteristically show no neutrophils), are common in LAD1
evidence.explanation: The histological point that the lesions are neutrophil-free, which both supports the node and corrects a common misdiagnosis.

steps/9.description: Recurrent, severe, often life-threatening bacterial and fungal infection of skin and mucosal surfaces, with the diagnostically important feature that lesions do not suppurate. Necrotic skin lesions in LAD1 are frequently labelled pyoderma gangrenosum, which is a misreading - the biopsy characteristically contains no neutrophils at all, which is the opposite of what that diagnosis implies.

evidence.snippet: Delayed umbilical cord separation was found in 25 patients (36.2%).
evidence.explanation: The cohort frequency, which is the basis for the FREQUENT band rather than a higher one.

evidence.snippet: Delayed is defined as umbilical cord separation after 21 days of life.
evidence.explanation: The threshold the consensus criteria use, which is what makes this a recordable diagnostic criterion rather than an impression.

steps/10.description: Separation of the umbilical cord later than 21 days of life, often with omphalitis. This is frequently the first clinical sign and is one of the presenting features that should prompt integrin flow cytometry. It is not universal - a 69-patient series recorded it in 36.2% - so its absence does not exclude the diagnosis, which is the reverse of how the sign is often taught.

evidence.snippet: Skin ulcers (75.4%), omphalitis (65.2%), and gingivitis (37.7%) were the most frequent complaints.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies omphalitis at 65.2% in the largest single-centre LAD-I series, supporting the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Omphalitis was considered the most frequent symptom in patients aged <6 months (87.5%; n = 7/8)
evidence.explanation: Expert-consensus ranking of omphalitis as the leading early presentation. Note the percentage is the proportion of panellists agreeing, not a patient frequency.

steps/11.description: Infection of the umbilical stump, rated by the consensus panel as the single most common presenting manifestation below six months of age and recorded in 65.2% of a 69-patient series.

evidence.snippet: resulting in severe recurrent nonpussing infections and neutrophilia, often preceded by delayed separation of the umbilical cord
evidence.explanation: States the non-suppurative character of the infections directly, alongside the neutrophilia and cord sign.

evidence.snippet: Skin ulcers (75.4%), omphalitis (65.2%), and gingivitis (37.7%) were the most frequent complaints.
evidence.explanation: Skin ulceration in 75.4% of the cohort, the most frequent single complaint, supporting the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/12.description: Recurrent severe infection of skin and mucosal surfaces - and, later, the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts - that is necrotic rather than suppurative. The absence of pus in a clinically severe infection is the feature that most reliably distinguishes this disease from other phagocyte defects at the bedside, because it is a direct readout of the mechanism rather than a downstream complication.

evidence.snippet: Skin ulcers (75.4%), omphalitis (65.2%), and gingivitis (37.7%) were the most frequent complaints.
evidence.explanation: Places skin ulceration at 75.4%, the highest-frequency manifestation in the cohort.

evidence.snippet: Chronic necrotic skin lesions, often incorrectly described as pyoderma gangrenosum (biopsy samples characteristically show no neutrophils), are common in LAD1
evidence.explanation: Characterises the lesions as common, chronic and neutrophil-free, and flags the recurring misdiagnosis.

steps/13.description: Persistent necrotic skin ulcers that enlarge despite antibiotics and debridement. Often labelled pyoderma gangrenosum, but the histology is the opposite of that diagnosis - the biopsy characteristically contains no neutrophils.

evidence.snippet: Recurrent oral ulcers cause severe pain and difficulty eating, and severe periodontitis leads to complete loss of adult teeth in almost all patients.
evidence.explanation: States both the severity and the near-universal outcome, which is the basis for the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Periodontitis with severe loss of tooth-supporting connective tissue and bone was clinically diagnosed in all patients in our LAD-I cohort
evidence.explanation: Every patient in a characterised LAD-I cohort had it, which is the direct cohort support for treating this as near-universal.

steps/14.description: Generalised aggressive periodontitis beginning in childhood, with attachment loss, alveolar bone destruction and eventual loss of both primary and permanent teeth. Described as invariable in affected individuals, and as leading to complete loss of adult teeth in almost all patients. It is refractory to conventional periodontal care, which is a consequence of the mechanism curated above rather than a failure of treatment.

evidence.snippet: invariably develop early-onset generalized aggressive periodontitis featuring severe bone loss and premature loss of primary and permanent teeth
evidence.explanation: Names premature loss of permanent teeth as part of the invariable periodontal course.

steps/15.description: Loss of the permanent dentition in adolescence or early adulthood, following the periodontal bone destruction. Recorded separately from the periodontitis itself because it is the endpoint families experience and the outcome that anti-inflammatory therapy is aimed at preventing.

evidence.snippet: Characteristic features are delayed separation of the umbilical cord and strong leukocytosis, especially neutrophilia, during periods of infection.
evidence.explanation: States marked leukocytosis with neutrophilia as a characteristic feature.

evidence.snippet: Pretreatment neutrophilia and skin abnormalities related to LAD-I resolved.
evidence.explanation: The neutrophilia resolving once CD18 is restored, which confirms it is secondary to the adhesion defect rather than an independent marrow phenotype.

steps/16.description: A persistently high circulating leukocyte and neutrophil count, rising further during infection and often reaching values that would suggest leukaemia in another context. It is the most counterintuitive finding in the disease and the one most likely to mislead - the count is high precisely because the cells cannot get to where they are needed. It normalises after successful HSCT or gene therapy, which is the cleanest demonstration that it is a consequence of the adhesion defect.

evidence.snippet: LAD-I severity has historically been classified by the percentage of CD18+ polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) in peripheral blood, with <2% indicating a severe phenotype and ≥2% but <30% indicating a moderate phenotype.
evidence.explanation: The thresholds themselves, which is what makes this a graded diagnostic measurement rather than a binary one.

evidence.snippet: Forty-six patients (66.7%) were categorized as severe (CD18 and/or CD11a: below 2%); while 23 children (33.3%) were in moderate category (CD18 and/or CD11a: 2%-30%).
evidence.explanation: The severity distribution observed when the threshold is applied to a real cohort.

steps/17.description: Flow cytometry of peripheral neutrophils showing absent or reduced surface CD18, with a matching reduction in CD11a and CD11b. This is the defining diagnostic test and also the severity metric - below 2% of expected CD18 defines severe disease and 2-30% defines moderate disease. In one 69-patient series two thirds were severe by this criterion. The measurement is not always sufficient on its own: a patient may express near-normal but non-functional protein, which is why the consensus pairs flow cytometry with ITGB2 sequencing.

evidence.snippet: In particular, two of them developed renal and intestinal autoimmune diseases, despite the expression of Beta-2 integrin was partially conserved.
evidence.explanation: Documents autoimmune disease in molecularly confirmed LAD-1 patients, including in those with partial integrin expression.

evidence.snippet: suggesting that HSCT is effective for preventing infections in LAD-1, but does not prevent the risk of the autoimmune complications
evidence.explanation: The post-transplant persistence, which is the clinically important part of this phenotype and the reason it is curated separately from the infection phenotype.

steps/18.description: Autoimmune disease - renal, intestinal, type 1 diabetes, autoimmune cytopenia - reported in a long-term follow-up series both in untreated patients and after HSCT. Recorded because it is a genuinely under-recognised part of the natural history: it occurred in patients whose beta-2 integrin expression was partially preserved, and transplantation corrected the infection risk without abolishing it.

evidence.snippet: Mutant beta subunit precursors from LAD patients failed to associate with the LFA-1 alpha subunit.
evidence.explanation: The assembly failure itself, measured on patient-derived precursors - this is the step that connects the genotype to the receptor-family defect.

edges/1.description: The gene product is the shared beta chain, so a disabling variant removes the assembly partner directly.

edges/2.description: The flow-cytometry measurement of this node, and the test the diagnosis is made on — surface CD18 is absent or reduced because the heterodimer never assembles.

evidence.snippet: the β2 integrins are required for the adhesion of neutrophils to endothelium and the transmigration of neutrophils into tissues
evidence.explanation: States that the receptors lost at this node are the ones required for the adhesion and transmigration steps below it.

edges/3.description: The absent heterodimers are the receptors that mediate firm arrest, so losing them removes the interaction.

evidence.snippet: The LFA-1 integrin (CD11a/CD18) plays a crucial role in firm adhesion, which is essential to the subsequent extravasation of the neutrophils to peripheral tissues
evidence.explanation: States the ordering explicitly - firm adhesion is the prerequisite for extravasation, which is what makes this an edge rather than two parallel defects.

edges/4.description: Transmigration is downstream of firm arrest in the adhesion cascade, so a cell that never arrests never crosses.

edges/5.description: Neutrophils that cannot leave the circulation accumulate in the compartment they are counted in and are missing from the one they are needed in.

edges/6.description: Wound repair requires neutrophil recruitment into the wound bed, which does not occur.

edges/7.description: The blood-count half of that dissociation. Counts are often extreme, and a high count here indicates the disease rather than excluding it.

edges/8.description: Pus is accumulated tissue neutrophils; with none arriving, infection proceeds without it.

evidence.snippet: The disruption of this circuit as a result of the paucity of tissue neutrophils in LAD1 leads to exaggerated interleukin-23 and interleukin-17 responses, which appear to account for local LAD1 immunopathologic processes.
evidence.explanation: Names tissue neutrophil paucity as the cause of the cytokine dysregulation, which is exactly this edge.

edges/9.description: The absent tissue neutrophils are the input to the efferocytosis feedback loop that normally restrains IL-23 production.

edges/10.description: The defining infection phenotype: necrosis without the purulence that requires neutrophils to arrive in tissue.

edges/11.description: Infection of the umbilical stump, classically the first presentation in the neonatal period.

edges/12.description: Autoimmune and inflammatory complications arising from the dysregulated barrier-site axis rather than from the adhesion defect directly.

evidence.snippet: Local treatment with antibodies to IL-17 or IL-23 in LFA-1-deficient mice not only blocked inflammatory periodontal bone loss but also caused a reduction in the total bacterial burden
evidence.explanation: An intervention result, which is what establishes the link as causal rather than correlative. Graded MODEL_ORGANISM because the intervention was done in mice - the equivalent experiment has not been run in patients.

edges/13.description: IL-17 is an osteoclastogenic cytokine, and blocking it or its IL-23 driver prevents the bone loss in the corresponding mouse model.

edges/14.description: The periodontium depends on continuous neutrophil traffic, which is why it fails first and hardest in every adhesion defect.

edges/15.description: The endpoint of that bone loss.

edges/16.description: Cord separation depends on neutrophil-mediated tissue remodelling, so delay beyond three weeks is an early and characteristic sign.

edges/17.description: The same remodelling failure in skin, producing ulcers that persist rather than close.

evidence.snippet: In LAD-I, mutations are found in ITGB2, the gene that encodes the β subunit of the β(2) integrins.
evidence.explanation: The gene-disease assignment from the curated mutation compendium for this disease.

evidence.snippet: Usually, this leads to the absence or decreased expression of the β2 integrins on the leukocyte surface, but sometimes a normal expression of nonfunctional β2 integrins is found.
evidence.explanation: The exception that makes CD18 flow cytometry alone insufficient - normal expression of non-functional receptor.

evidence.snippet: Most of the point mutations are found in a ~240-residue domain that is highly conserved in all β integrin subunits and coded for by exons 5 – 9 of ITGB2
evidence.explanation: The variant distribution across the gene, which is what makes exons 5-9 the high-yield region on sequencing.

genes/0.notes: ITGB2 at 21q22.3 encodes CD18, the beta-2 integrin subunit. Two things about the allelic spectrum matter clinically. First, the severity gradient is quantitative - residual surface CD18 sets the phenotype, and the same gene produces everything from neonatal lethal disease to a presentation deferred into adolescence. Second, reduced surface expression is the usual but not the only mechanism: a normal amount of non-functional protein occurs, which is why the consensus recommends CD11a/CD11b measurement and ITGB2 sequencing alongside CD18 flow cytometry rather than relying on the CD18 number alone. Most missense variants fall in the conserved betaI domain encoded by exons 5-9, which carries the ligand-binding MIDAS motif.

evidence.snippet: The curative treatment of LAD-I and LAD-III is allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT).
evidence.explanation: States allo-HSCT as the curative treatment for this disease.

evidence.snippet: The 3-year overall survival estimate (95% confidence interval [CI]) was 83% (74-92) for the entire cohort: 84% (75-94) and 75% (50-100) for LAD-I and LAD-III, respectively.
evidence.explanation: The survival outcome from the largest transplant series in this disease.

evidence.snippet: We observed cumulative incidences (95% CI) of graft failure (GF) at 3 years of 17% (9%-26%) and grade II to IV acute graft-versus-host disease (aGVHD) at 100 days of 24% (15%-34%).
evidence.explanation: The complication rates, which are the reason this is curative but not straightforward and why gene therapy is being developed.

evidence.snippet: The overall survival of patients with and without hematopoietic stem cell transplantation was 79.3% and 55.6%, respectively.
evidence.explanation: A within-cohort comparison of transplanted against non-transplanted patients. Note this is an observational contrast, not a randomised one, so selection effects are not excluded.

treatments/0.description: The established curative treatment for severe LAD-I, replacing the patient's CD18-deficient haematopoiesis with donor cells that express functional beta-2 integrins. The largest outcome series is an EBMT registry cohort of 84 LAD-I and LAD-III patients transplanted between 2007 and 2017, with 3-year overall survival of 83%. The event-free figure is considerably lower and is where the real difficulty lies: 17% graft failure at 3 years and 24% grade II-IV acute GVHD at 100 days, with acute GVHD a significant risk factor for death. Outcomes are better in younger patients, which is why the consensus asks for transplantation as soon as possible after diagnosis and ideally at or before 13 months of age. The registry authors argue that LAD's own inflammatory component contributes to these transplant complications, which is the rationale for anti-inflammatory pretreatment.

evidence.snippet: successful bone marrow transplantation in LAD-I patients reverses the periodontal disease phenotype
evidence.explanation: A downstream node of the pathograph reversing after transplantation, which is the clinical demonstration that correcting the molecular lesion corrects the chain.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Donor-derived leukocytes carry wild-type ITGB2, so the assembly defect is replaced rather than bypassed - which is why the correction is durable and why the entire downstream chain resolves together.

evidence.snippet: HSCT-free survival was 100% (95% confidence interval [CI], 66 to 100) at 1 year after infusion (P<0.001).
evidence.explanation: The primary efficacy result of the phase 1-2 study.

evidence.snippet: Serious adverse events related to myeloablative busulfan conditioning were observed. No adverse events attributed to gene therapy were reported. None of the patients had graft failure.
evidence.explanation: The safety profile, and the attribution of serious events to conditioning rather than to the product.

evidence.snippet: In this study, lentiviral vector-transduced autologous CD34+ HSCT was successful in treating severe LAD-I.
evidence.explanation: The authors' conclusion. Note the cohort is nine children with 24 months of follow-up, so this establishes feasibility and short-term efficacy rather than equivalence to allogeneic transplantation.

treatments/1.description: Autologous CD34+ haematopoietic stem cells transduced ex vivo with a self-inactivating lentiviral vector carrying human ITGB2, given after myeloablative busulfan conditioning. The point of the approach is that it removes the two problems that limit allogeneic transplantation in this disease - donor availability and alloreactivity - and the phase 1-2 result bears that out: nine children with severe LAD-I, no graft failure, no adverse events attributed to the gene therapy itself, and 100% HSCT-free survival at one year. Serious adverse events were attributable to the busulfan conditioning rather than to the product, which is the expected pattern and the remaining cost of the approach.

evidence.snippet: a gene therapy of autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem cells transduced with a self-inactivating lentiviral vector containing human ITGB2
evidence.explanation: Describes the product as delivering ITGB2 itself, which is what makes this an intervention on the initiating node.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Adds a functional ITGB2 transgene to the patient's own stem cells, correcting the initiating lesion in situ rather than replacing the haematopoietic system.

evidence.snippet: After 1 year of therapy, our patient had resolution of his inflammatory lesions without serious infections or adverse reactions.
evidence.explanation: The clinical outcome in the index case, with the safety observation that matters most in an immunodeficient patient.

evidence.snippet: By 10 to 14 months, the wound was completely healed with minimal residual scarring
evidence.explanation: Healing of a wound that had progressed for two years through antibiotics and repeated debridement, which is the strongest single observation in the report.

evidence.snippet: For all patients with LAD-I, anti-inflammatory therapy (eg, ustekinumab) should be prescribed as part of supportive care to treat dysregulated hyperinflammatory component of disease pathology (eg, chronic inflammation).
evidence.explanation: Moves this from a single case report to a consensus recommendation, which is why it is curated as a treatment rather than as an experimental observation.

treatments/2.description: Ustekinumab binds the p40 subunit shared by IL-12 and IL-23 and so shuts down the IL-23-driven IL-17 response that produces the periodontal and cutaneous immunopathology. This is a mechanism-directed treatment rather than an empirical one - the target was chosen from the observation that LAD1 lesions carry an IL-23/IL-17 signature and that blocking that axis prevents bone loss in the corresponding mouse model. In the index case, psoriasis dosing produced resolution of refractory gingival inflammation and complete healing of a two-year non-healing sacral wound within 10 to 14 months. The 2026 consensus now recommends anti-inflammatory therapy of this kind as part of supportive care, and before transplantation to help engraftment.

evidence.snippet: Levels of tissue markers of inflammation, such as interleukin-23 and interleukin-17, went from being very high relative to levels found in volunteers with healthy gingiva and patients with chronic periodontitis
evidence.explanation: Shows the drug acting on the node it targets, measured in the tissue rather than inferred from the clinical response.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Blocks the shared p40 subunit, removing the IL-23 signal that drives the IL-17 response. It treats the disinhibited inflammatory arm and does nothing for the adhesion defect itself, so it is adjunctive rather than definitive.

evidence.snippet: All patients with severe LAD-I require prophylactic antimicrobials (ie, antibiotics, antifungals).
evidence.explanation: The consensus recommendation for universal antimicrobial prophylaxis in severe disease.

evidence.snippet: Infections in patients with severe LAD-I often require prolonged antimicrobial treatment, including multiple courses of antimicrobials.
evidence.explanation: Characterises the intensity of treatment required, which is part of the burden of illness this entry records.

evidence.snippet: We observed progressive periodontal disease in all patients evaluated, despite prophylactic antibiotic use since infancy and access to dental care.
evidence.explanation: Refutes any claim that antimicrobial prophylaxis controls the periodontal arm of the disease. Recorded here rather than omitted because the limit of this treatment is clinically load-bearing - it is what motivates the anti-inflammatory approach.

treatments/3.description: Continuous antibacterial and antifungal prophylaxis, with hospital-based aggressive management and often prolonged or repeated courses for intercurrent infection. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the prophylactic agent in the published cases. This is the standard of care while awaiting definitive therapy, and its limits are well documented - prophylaxis since infancy did not prevent progressive periodontal disease in any patient in the characterised cohort, because the periodontal arm is inflammatory rather than infective.

treatments/3/targets/0.description: Reduces microbial burden to compensate for the missing neutrophil response. It does not restore neutrophil delivery, so it is compensatory rather than corrective.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, the prenatal diagnosis would benefit families with a history of LAD-I.
evidence.explanation: The cohort study's own recommendation for prenatal diagnosis in affected families.

treatments/4.description: Autosomal recessive inheritance carries a 25% recurrence risk per pregnancy for carrier couples. Because consanguinity is common in the reported families and ITGB2 sequencing is established, carrier testing and prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis are informative where the family allele is known. Molecular confirmation also has a direct therapeutic consequence here: genetic diagnosis is best practice before allogeneic transplantation and mandatory before gene therapy.

open_questions/0.rationale:
For decades the answer was assumed to be the first, and it is the intuitive reading - neutrophils cannot reach the gingival sulcus, so the bacteria win. Three observations do not fit. Bacterial load inside the diseased gingival tissue is comparable to or lower than in healthy controls. The infiltrate is dense but lymphocytic, with neutrophils visible confined inside vessels. And prophylactic antibiotics from infancy plus dental care did not prevent progression in any patient evaluated.
The alternative reading explains all three. Efferocytosis of transmigrated apoptotic neutrophils is the signal that tells tissue macrophages to stop making IL-23. Remove the transmigration and the signal never arrives, so a physiological response to the oral microbiome runs without a brake and IL-17 drives osteoclastic bone loss. On this reading the bacteria are the stimulus rather than the agent, which is why suppressing them incompletely - as antibiotics do at a mucosal surface - changes nothing.
The distinction is not academic. It predicts that blocking the axis should work where antimicrobials do not, and blocking it did: anti-IL-17 and anti-IL-23 prevented bone loss in LFA-1-deficient mice, and ustekinumab resolved refractory periodontal inflammation in a patient. It also suggests the same logic may apply at other barrier sites in this disease, and in other conditions where neutrophils fail to reach tissue.

open_questions/1.rationale:
The severe subtype has a defined prognosis and a definitive treatment recommendation. Moderate LAD-I has neither. The consensus asks for routine reassessment precisely because severity is understood to sit on a spectrum and to be able to progress, but it offers no predictor of who progresses, over what interval, or what should trigger a move to definitive therapy.
Two observations make this more than a bookkeeping gap. Residual CD18 does not protect the periodontium proportionally - attachment loss scales inversely with remaining CD18, so moderate patients still lose their dentition. And the autoimmune complications reported in long-term follow-up occurred in patients whose beta-2 integrin expression was partially conserved, which is to say in the moderate range. A subtype defined by a laboratory threshold that does not predict its own major morbidities is a subtype whose boundary needs re-examining.
Answering this needs prospective follow-up of a moderate cohort with periodontal, autoimmune and infection endpoints, which no published series provides.

open_questions/2.rationale:
The phase 1-2 gene therapy result is striking on its own terms - nine children, no graft failure, 100% HSCT-free survival at one year - and it removes the two things that make allogeneic transplantation difficult here, donor availability and alloreactivity. But the comparison that clinicians need has not been made. The allogeneic registry cohort is 84 patients with three-year outcomes; the gene therapy cohort is nine with two years of follow-up, and a cross-study comparison of those two is not a comparison.
Two specific questions are open. First, durability: beta-2 integrin expression must be maintained in the myeloid compartment for life, and the threshold fraction of corrected cells needed to hold the phenotype is not established from human data. Second, whether gene therapy addresses the non-infectious arms of the disease - the autoimmune complications seen after allogeneic transplantation, and the periodontal disease - or only the infection burden that both the primary endpoint and the reported outcomes emphasise.

evidence.snippet: Advances in our understanding of the pathophysiology of lupus nephritis have provided insights into the mechanisms by which the impaired clearance of nuclear self-antigens drives innate immune activation
evidence.explanation: Identifies impaired nuclear self-antigen clearance as the upstream mechanism initiating innate immune activation in lupus nephritis.

steps/0.description: Apoptotic cells and the nuclear material they release are cleared inefficiently in SLE, so nucleosomes, chromatin and DNA persist in the extracellular space instead of being disposed of by phagocytes. This persistence is the upstream lesion that exposes innate nucleic-acid sensors to self-derived ligands.

evidence.snippet: impaired clearance of nuclear self-antigens drives innate immune activation, including excessive Toll-like receptor signalling, interferon pathway upregulation and B cell hyperactivation
evidence.explanation: Identifies excessive Toll-like receptor signalling as a component of innate immune activation in lupus nephritis.

steps/1.description: Uncleared nuclear self-antigens engage endosomal nucleic-acid-sensing Toll-like receptors on plasmacytoid dendritic cells and other innate cells, driving signalling above its normal set point.

evidence.snippet: impaired clearance of nuclear self-antigens drives innate immune activation, including excessive Toll-like receptor signalling, interferon pathway upregulation and B cell hyperactivation
evidence.explanation: Identifies interferon pathway upregulation as a component of innate immune activation in lupus nephritis.

steps/2.description: Type I interferon signalling is upregulated downstream of nucleic-acid-driven Toll-like receptor engagement, lowering the activation threshold of B cells and other lymphocytes and sustaining the autoimmune response.

evidence.snippet: impaired clearance of nuclear self-antigens drives innate immune activation, including excessive Toll-like receptor signalling, interferon pathway upregulation and B cell hyperactivation
evidence.explanation: Identifies B cell hyperactivation as the terminal component of the innate activation cascade in lupus nephritis.

steps/3.description: B cells are activated above their normal threshold in the interferon-rich, self-antigen-rich environment established upstream. This is the step at which the innate cascade converts into the adaptive, autoantibody-producing arm of disease.

evidence.snippet: Antibodies to dsDNA/nucleosomes are most closely linked with development of nephritis
evidence.explanation: Identifies anti-dsDNA/nucleosome antibodies as the autoantibody species most associated with lupus nephritis.

evidence.snippet: anti-DNA antibody structures and anti-chromatin antibodies; their origins, and their impact on operational molecular and cellular processes accounting for lupus nephritis
evidence.explanation: Situates chromatin-directed autoantibodies at the center of the molecular and cellular processes producing lupus nephritis.

evidence.snippet: These processes sustain autoantibody production and complement activation and contribute to progressive tissue injury
evidence.explanation: Supports autoantibody production as a central mechanism sustained by TLR signaling and interferon pathway upregulation in lupus nephritis.

steps/4.description: Failure of B-cell tolerance in SLE, driven by innate immune activation through impaired nuclear antigen clearance and excessive Toll-like receptor signaling, generates anti-dsDNA and anti-chromatin (anti-nucleosome) autoantibodies from hyperactivated autoreactive B cells and plasma cells. These antibodies to DNA/nucleosomes are the autoantibody species most closely linked to the development of nephritis and form circulating and in-situ immune complexes.

evidence.snippet: anti-dsDNA/chromatin antibodies binding to nucleosomes/DNA present in the glomerular matrix, as the most compelling
evidence.explanation: Supports the in-situ binding mechanism of glomerular immune-complex formation.

steps/5.description: Immune complexes accumulate in the glomerulus both by deposition of circulating complexes and by in-situ binding of anti-dsDNA/chromatin antibodies to nucleosomes and DNA present in the glomerular matrix, engaging mesangial cells, glomerular endothelium, and podocytes across the mesangial, subendothelial, and subepithelial compartments that define the ISN/RPS histologic classes.

evidence.snippet: Deposition of complement proteins in glomeruli is a key feature of lupus nephritis.
evidence.explanation: Establishes glomerular complement deposition as a defining feature of lupus nephritis.

evidence.snippet: When anti-C1q antibodies are present along with anti-dsDNA antibodies, development of renal disease is accelerated
evidence.explanation: Supports anti-C1q antibodies as an accelerant of complement-driven renal disease.

evidence.snippet: These processes sustain autoantibody production and complement activation and contribute to progressive tissue injury
evidence.explanation: Supports complement activation as a mechanism sustained by the upstream innate cascade and contributing to progressive tissue injury.

steps/6.description: Glomerular immune complexes activate the complement cascade — deposition of complement proteins in glomeruli is a hallmark of lupus nephritis — and recruit macrophages and other leukocytes, producing an inflammatory glomerular microenvironment. Concurrent anti-C1q antibodies accelerate renal disease.

evidence.snippet: low oxygen tension and hypertonicity) and unique kidney cell types affect the intrarenal immune cells in LN
evidence.explanation: Identifies low oxygen tension and hypertonicity as the biochemical environment of the kidney in this model.

steps/7.description: The kidney's distinctive biochemical environment — the low oxygen tension of the corticomedullary gradient and the hypertonicity of the medullary interstitium — is a constitutive feature of normal renal physiology, not a state induced by lupus. It is modelled here as an initiating, contextual node because it is the pre-existing environment that infiltrating immune cells arrive into, and it shapes how those cells behave once they are there. It therefore carries no incoming edge from the immune infiltrate.

evidence.snippet: The pathways used by intrinsic renal cells to interact with immune cells, such as antigen presentation and cytokine production
evidence.explanation: Establishes that intrinsic renal cells engage immune cells through antigen presentation and cytokine production.

steps/8.description: Intrinsic renal cells are not passive bystanders to the infiltrate. They interact with intrarenal immune cells through defined pathways — notably antigen presentation and cytokine production — and so participate directly in local immune regulation. Unlike the biochemical niche, this activity is induced by, and downstream of, the intrarenal immune infiltrate.

evidence.snippet: the kidney microenvironment influences the recruitment, survival, differentiation, and activation of immune cells
evidence.explanation: Supports kidney-directed conditioning of intrarenal immune cell recruitment, survival, differentiation, and activation.

steps/9.description: The convergent output of the renal niche and of intrinsic renal cell engagement: the recruitment, survival, differentiation, and activation of the immune cells within the kidney are shaped by the kidney itself. This is the node at which the causal direction reverses relative to the classical cascade, and it feeds back onto both the infiltrate that supplied the cells and the renal cells that conditioned them.

evidence.snippet: which, in turn, modify kidney cell function
evidence.explanation: States that the kidney-conditioned immune cells modify kidney cell function.

steps/10.description: The endpoint of the reciprocal arm: intrinsic renal cell function is modified by the immune cells the kidney has conditioned. Modelling this explicitly keeps both halves of the review's reciprocal claim as their own edges rather than leaving the kidney-directed half implicit, and it is the route by which the crosstalk loop contributes to tissue damage.

evidence.snippet: The pathologic classes vary from mild mesangial involvement (Class I) to diffuse proliferative disease (Class IV) to membranous disease (Class V) to end-stage fibrosis (Class VI).
evidence.explanation: Describes the graded histopathologic spectrum of glomerular injury in lupus nephritis.

evidence.snippet: End-stage renal disease in lupus is secondary to loss of glomerular and tubular function due to renal cell death and resultant fibrosis.
evidence.explanation: Links glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury to end-stage renal disease.

steps/11.description: Sustained immune-complex, complement, and inflammatory injury produces the graded ISN/RPS histologic spectrum — from mesangial (class I/II) through proliferative (class III/IV) and membranous (class V) disease to end-stage fibrosis (class VI) — with tubulointerstitial disease that also impacts prognosis. Loss of glomerular and tubular function through renal cell death and fibrosis underlies progression to end-stage kidney disease.

evidence.snippet: The kidney in LN is characterized by a significant immune infiltrate and proinflammatory cytokine milieu
evidence.explanation: Supports the intrarenal immune infiltrate and cytokine milieu as a defining feature of the lupus kidney.

steps/12.description: Downstream of complement and Fc-receptor activation, the lupus kidney accumulates a substantial infiltrate of T cells, macrophages, and other leukocytes together with a proinflammatory cytokine milieu. This intrarenal compartment is not merely a bystander readout of systemic autoimmunity: the infiltrating cells and the cytokines they produce act directly on intrinsic renal cells, and are in part responsible for the tissue damage seen in lupus nephritis.

treatments/1.description: Glucocorticoids are a backbone of both induction and maintenance immunosuppression in lupus nephritis.

evidence.explanation: REGENCY trial conclusion supporting obinutuzumab as an approved lupus nephritis therapy.

treatments/4.description: Obinutuzumab, a type II anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, added to standard mycophenolate-plus-glucocorticoid therapy, is the most recently approved (2025) lupus nephritis-specific agent, based on the phase 3 REGENCY trial, which met its primary endpoint of complete renal response at week 76.

evidence.snippet: It is now increasingly appreciated that LN is not due to unidirectional immune cell activation with subsequent kidney damage.
evidence.explanation: This review does not dispute that immune-complex-driven activation causes renal injury, but holds the strictly unidirectional framing to be an incomplete account of lupus nephritis — hence PARTIAL rather than SUPPORT for the model as a whole.

hypotheses/0.description: The classical account treats the kidney as a passive target of systemic autoimmunity: autoreactive B cells and plasma cells generate anti-dsDNA and anti-chromatin antibodies, the resulting immune complexes deposit in — or bind in situ within — the glomerulus, and complement, Fc-receptor, and Toll-like-receptor engagement drive inflammatory glomerular and tubulointerstitial injury. Causal flow runs in one direction, from systemic autoimmunity to renal tissue damage, and this model underwrites systemic immunosuppression as the therapeutic strategy.

evidence.snippet: the kidney microenvironment influences the recruitment, survival, differentiation, and activation of immune cells, which, in turn, modify kidney cell function
evidence.explanation: States the reciprocal kidney-to-immune-cell and immune-cell-to-kidney arms that define this model.

hypotheses/1.description: An extension in which the kidney is an active participant rather than a passive target. The renal biochemical niche (low oxygen tension and hypertonicity) together with intrinsic renal cell types — which can present antigen and produce cytokines — shapes the recruitment, survival, differentiation, and activation of the intrarenal immune infiltrate; those conditioned immune cells in turn modify kidney cell function, closing a self-amplifying loop. The model does not replace the immune-complex cascade; it adds a reciprocal arm downstream of it, and it predicts that kidney-targeted rather than systemic intervention could interrupt the loop.

evidence.snippet: An understanding of these mechanisms can lead to the design of more kidney-targeted treatments and the avoidance of systemic immunosuppressive effects and may represent the next frontier of LN therapies.
evidence.explanation: Frames kidney-targeted therapy as a prospective consequence of these mechanisms ("can lead to", "may represent"), i.e. an open question rather than a demonstrated therapeutic result.

open_questions/0.rationale: Every treatment currently curated on this entry — mycophenolate/cyclophosphamide induction, corticosteroids, belimumab, voclosporin, obinutuzumab, rituximab, azathioprine — acts systemically, which follows from the unidirectional model in which the kidney is a passive target. If the reciprocal arm is a genuine driver, the loop is in principle interruptible at renal-restricted nodes (the hypoxic and hypertonic niche, renal antigen presentation, renal cytokine production) that systemic immunosuppression does not specifically address. The gap is that no kidney-targeted agent acting on these nodes has been shown to change renal outcomes in patients, so the therapeutic claim remains a prediction of the model rather than a curated treatment.

steps/3.description: During transmission, Borrelia burgdorferi co-opts components of Ixodes tick saliva to establish infection at the bite site. The spirochete selectively enhances tick expression of the 15-kDa salivary protein Salp15, which binds the spirochetal surface lipoprotein OspC and coats the organism. Salp15 (and its I. ricinus homologue Iric1) shields Borrelia from antibody-mediated killing and complement, giving the spirochete a marked infectivity advantage in the mammalian host; the bacterium thereby exploits a secreted arthropod protein to colonize the vertebrate dermis.

evidence.snippet: The ribosome is one of the main antibiotic targets in the bacterial cell.

steps/4.description: Borrelia burgdorferi depends on 70S-ribosome translation. Doxycycline, the first-line agent for early localized and early disseminated Lyme disease, binds the 30S subunit and arrests bacterial protein synthesis — a ribosomal target distinct from the PBP target of the beta-lactam alternatives.

evidence.snippet: although glycan chain polymerization occurs in the absence of transpeptidation (for example, in the presence of penicillin), efficient transpeptidation requires ongoing GTase reactions

steps/5.description: Borrelia burgdorferi maintains its peptidoglycan cell wall by penicillin-binding protein (PBP) transpeptidase cross-linking. This essential, bacteria-specific reaction is the target of the amoxicillin and ceftriaxone used to treat Lyme disease; beta-lactam acylation of the PBP active site halts cross-linking and is bactericidal against disseminating spirochetes. CNS penetration of ceftriaxone is what extends this mechanism to neuroborreliosis.

evidence.snippet: B. burgdorferi expresses outer surface protein A (OspA) but not OspC when residing in the midgut of unfed ticks. However, after ticks feed on blood, some spirochetes stop making OspA and express OspC.
evidence.explanation: Immunofluorescence of spirochetes in feeding Ixodes nymphs demonstrates the reciprocal OspA-to-OspC switch that accompanies transmission from tick to mammal.

evidence.snippet: we integrate this large body of information into a cohesive picture of the molecular and cellular events that transpire as Lyme disease spirochaetes transit between their arthropod and vertebrate hosts during the enzootic cycle.
evidence.explanation: Authoritative review frames B. burgdorferi pathogenesis around its dual-host transit between Ixodes ticks and vertebrate hosts during the enzootic cycle.

steps/6.description: Borrelia burgdorferi is maintained in an enzootic cycle between Ixodes ticks and small-mammal reservoirs such as the white-footed mouse; larval ticks acquire spirochetes by feeding on infected reservoirs and transmit them transstadially to the nymphal stage that bites humans. In the unfed tick midgut the spirochete expresses OspA (midgut adhesion) but not OspC. During the blood meal, host- and temperature-derived signals trigger a reciprocal antigenic switch in which OspA is downregulated and OspC is upregulated, accompanying spirochete migration from the midgut to the salivary glands and transmission into the vertebrate dermis; OspC expression peaks around 48 h of tick attachment and is required for early mammalian infectivity.

evidence.snippet: BBK32 binds to C1r, the initiator protease of the classical pathway of complement, and protects B. burgdorferi from complement-mediated killing following exposure to normal human serum.
evidence.explanation: Functional in vitro evidence that BBK32 binds C1r and blocks classical-pathway complement killing of infectious Borrelia burgdorferi.

steps/7.description: The Borrelia burgdorferi surface lipoprotein BBK32 binds C1r, the initiator protease of the classical complement pathway. This attenuates antibody-dependent complement activation and protects infectious Borrelia from complement-mediated killing in human serum.

evidence.snippet: the CspA-mediated binding of human FH confers serum resistance by directly inhibiting complement deposition on the surface of B. burgdorferi.
evidence.explanation: A cspA knockout loses surface factor H binding and becomes serum-sensitive with enhanced C3/C6/C5b-9 deposition, demonstrating CspA-driven alternative-pathway evasion.

steps/8.description: Borrelia burgdorferi expresses complement regulator-acquiring surface proteins (CRASPs) such as CspA (CRASP-1), along with CspZ and OspE-family paralogs, that bind the host alternative-pathway regulators factor H and factor H-like protein 1 (FH/FHL-1). Surface-bound FH/FHL-1 limits C3 deposition and membrane-attack-complex formation, conferring resistance to complement-mediated killing in human serum. This pathway complements the BBK32-mediated classical-pathway block.

evidence.snippet: Borrelia burgdorferi, the Lyme disease pathogen, has evolved an intricate antigenic variation mechanism to evade the host immune response, enabling its dissemination, persistence, and pathogenicity.
evidence.explanation: Mechanistic study of the vlsE locus confirms antigenic variation as the immune-evasion mechanism enabling B. burgdorferi persistence.

steps/9.description: The vlsE locus undergoes gene conversion that diversifies Borrelia surface antigens, helping the pathogen evade host immune recognition during dissemination and persistent infection.

evidence.explanation: Lipidomic study establishes B. burgdorferi as a lipid auxotroph dependent on host-derived lipids for survival.

evidence.explanation: The spirochete shows discriminatory lipid uptake, concentrating cholesteryl esters and triglycerides into intracellular foci.

evidence.snippet: the pathogen also synthesizes predominantly eukaryotic lipids such as the lysosomal bis(monoacylglycerol)phosphate and the plant glycolipid sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol (SQDG)
evidence.explanation: Despite its metabolic limitations, B. burgdorferi retains biosynthesis of eukaryotic-type lipids (BMP and SQDG).

evidence.explanation: The authors nominate lipid acquisition and biosynthesis pathways as survival-critical and therefore as potential antimicrobial targets.

evidence.explanation: SQDG biosynthesis is carried out by spirochetal enzymes (identified in the full text as BB0444 and BB0454) structurally homologous to plant SQD1/SQD2, supporting a residual eukaryotic-type biosynthetic capacity.

steps/10.description: Borrelia burgdorferi is a metabolically compromised spirochete (~1.5 Mbp genome) that cannot survive without host-derived lipids: it lacks de novo sterol synthesis and most lipid-biosynthetic capacity, requires exogenous cholesterol for growth and viability, and must scavenge lipids from the tick and vertebrate host to build and remodel its LPS-free, lipoprotein-rich cell envelope during the enzootic cycle. A multi-platform untargeted and targeted LC-MS/GC-MS lipidomic compendium detected more than 500 lipids in B. burgdorferi, the majority sourced from the environment through apparently discriminatory uptake (some species depleted 600-1500-fold during growth). The pathogen organizes neutral lipids — cholesteryl esters and triglycerides — into distinct intracellular foci (the first visual/molecular evidence of lipid-droplet-like storage in this minimal bacterium), and incorporates host sphingolipids and ceramides, with phosphatidylcholine established as a principal membrane constituent alongside cholesterol and cholesterol galactolipids (AcGal) that form cholesterol/sphingolipid lipid rafts. Unexpectedly, the spirochete also biosynthesizes predominantly eukaryotic lipids: four lysosomal bis(monoacylglycerol)phosphate (BMP) species (proposed roles in membrane plasticity/stress adaptation), phosphatidylglycerol and phosphatidylethanolamine, the plant galactolipid monogalactosyl diacylglycerol (MGDG; against which late-stage Lyme patients mount an antibody response), an acylated glycosylated phytosterol (acylhexosylcampesterol from scavenged campesterol), and the plant-type anionic sulfolipid sulfoquinovosyl diacylglycerol (SQDG). Structural-homology modeling against Arabidopsis SQD1/SQD2 and heterologous E. coli reconstitution identified two interdependent B. burgdorferi enzymes, BB0444 and BB0454, as sufficient for SQDG biosynthesis (BB0454 also makes MGDG); homologs are broadly conserved across spirochetes and >30 Borrelia species. This "lipid chimera" strategy of intensive scavenging plus niche biosynthesis is essential for envelope integrity and persistence, nominating lipid acquisition, sulfolipid synthesis, and neutral-lipid storage as candidate antimicrobial targets.

evidence.snippet: The clinical manifestations of Lyme disease range from a localized infection, for example, erythema migrans (EM) to a disseminated neurological or rheumatological infection, cardiac involvement, or even chronic disease.
evidence.explanation: Epidemiologic series shows Borrelia disseminates beyond skin to neurologic, rheumatologic, and cardiac sites.

steps/11.description: Borrelia burgdorferi is transmitted through Ixodes tick bites. The spirochete disseminates from the skin through the bloodstream to multiple organ systems including joints, heart, and nervous system. Surface adhesins like BBK32 and decorin-binding proteins (DbpA/DbpB) facilitate tissue colonization, while OspC is upregulated at the tick-feeding/early-mammalian interface and is required for early infectivity.

evidence.snippet: Aspiration of the left knee joint revealed a white cell count of 21.0×109/L (83% neutrophils) with negative Gram stain and culture. However, Lyme PCR was positive and accompanied by serologies consistent with Lyme arthritis.
evidence.explanation: Lyme arthritis joint fluid shows marked neutrophilic inflammation despite negative cultures, consistent with immune-driven damage.

steps/12.description: The host immune response to Borrelia antigens contributes to tissue damage. Spirochetal lipoproteins and peptidoglycan trigger robust innate immune activation with production of IL-6, IL-8, TNF, and chemokines (CCL3/CCL4). Persistent inflammation in joints may continue even after spirochete clearance.

evidence.snippet: long-term exposure of the host's immune system to spirochetes can contribute to the development of chronic autoimmune disease de novo.
evidence.explanation: Case review links persistent Borrelia exposure to downstream autoimmune disease.

steps/13.description: Prolonged exposure of the host immune system to Borrelia antigens can drive post-infectious autoimmunity, with reported triggers of systemic autoimmune disease after Lyme borreliosis.

evidence.snippet: We propose that ongoing PTLDS symptoms seem to be related to an autoimmune response to the tissue damage and inflammation caused by the viable or nonviable spirochete pathogen.
evidence.explanation: IDSA-aligned clinical review proposes post-infectious autoimmune/immune-dysregulation mechanisms for persistent PTLDS symptoms.

evidence.snippet: Receiver operating characteristic analysis identified a CCL19 cutoff of >111.67 pg/ml at 1 month following treatment completion to be 82% sensitive and 83% specific for later PTLDS.
evidence.explanation: Prospective cohort identifies persistently elevated posttreatment levels of the T-cell chemokine CCL19 as an immunologic risk marker for PTLDS, supporting ongoing immune-driven dysregulation rather than resolved infection.

steps/14.description: In an estimated 10-20% of appropriately treated patients, symptoms such as fatigue, pain, and cognitive complaints persist for more than six months (post-treatment Lyme disease syndrome, PTLDS). The mechanism is not fully established; proposed drivers include an autoimmune response to spirochete-induced tissue damage and inflammation, broader immune dysfunction, and persistent viable or nonviable antigen. This node is a terminal post-infectious state rather than ongoing high-burden active infection in most cases.

evidence.snippet: Results: In total, 1005 patients were enrolled with the following prevalence of clinical syndromes: erythema migrans (EM), 945 (94.02%); Lyme arthritis, 32 (3.18%); neuroborreliosis, 23 (2.28%); Lyme carditis, 4 (0.39%); and acrodermatitis, 1 (0.09%).

Season does not cause transmission and does not make it worse; it determines when in the year the questing nymphs that carry out transmission are available to do it. evidence.snippet: we present the case of Lyme's disease in an adult male with dog tick, Rhipecephalus as a vector.

The link is drawn because an atypical vector is still a transmission claim about this node, not because the case fits the cycle described there.

hypotheses/0.description: Lynch syndrome is caused by germline heterozygous loss-of-function variants in the DNA mismatch repair genes MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, or PMS2, or by EPCAM 3' deletions that silence MSH2 in epithelial tissue. Somatic biallelic MMR inactivation ('second hit') in intestinal, endometrial, and other epithelium produces microsatellite instability (MSI-H), accumulating insertion/deletion mutations at short tandem repeats and frameshift mutations in tumor suppressor genes (TGFBR2, BAX, MSH3) that drive colorectal, endometrial, ovarian, gastric, and urothelial carcinogenesis. The accelerated adenoma-carcinoma sequence in MMR-deficient colon (versus the Vogelstein chromosomal-instability path in FAP) explains the early-onset, right-sided, often poorly differentiated phenotype. MSI testing and IHC for MLH1/MSH2/MSH6/PMS2 are now standard tumor screening modalities. Immune checkpoint blockade (pembrolizumab, nivolumab) is highly effective in MSI-H tumors, corroborating that hypermutation-driven neoantigen load is mechanistically coupled to MMR loss and validates the MSI carcinogenesis axis of the canonical model.

genes/0.notes: Encodes myosin heavy chain IIa, the major isoform of fast type 2A fibres, in the skeletal myosin heavy chain cluster on chromosome 17p13. Dominant alleles are motor-domain (E706K) or distal-tail missense and splice variants; recessive alleles are truncating, splice, or missense variants. Sequencing of 50 control individuals found little coding variation in MYH2, consistent with strong selective constraint. ClinGen curates the two inheritance modes separately against MONDO:0011577: autosomal recessive as Definitive and autosomal dominant as Moderate, noting that a dominant-negative mechanism for the dominant form has been suggested but not established.
