genes/0.notes:
RFT1 (3p21.1) encodes a multispanning ER membrane protein with cytoplasmic N and C termini. The index allele is the homozygous missense c.199C>T (p.Arg67Cys); most RFT1-CDG alleles reported since map to regions of the protein conserved across eukaryotes, consistent with damage to a shared functional core. Note that human and yeast RFT1 share only about 22% sequence identity, so functional orthology had to be demonstrated experimentally by complementation rather than assumed from sequence.
Variant class and spectrum. Every RFT1-CDG allele reported is missense and biallelic; no null allele has been described, which is consistent with complete loss of RFT1 being incompatible with life. Alleles reported across the series include p.R67C (the index and recurrent allele), p.K152E and p.E298K (PMID:19701946), p.M408V and p.R442Q (PMID:23111317), and p.G276D, p.R25W and p.C70R (PMID:29923091), plus p.G340S (PMID:30071302).
Where the alleles fall. The three earliest-characterised alleles all sit in hydrophilic loops predicted to face the ER lumen, which is the structural observation behind reading these as damaging a shared translocation-relevant surface rather than being scattered. Later work identified p.G340S in a transmembrane helix instead, so luminal-loop localisation is a strong tendency and not a rule — a variant outside the loops is not thereby benign. The same structural point is used diagnostically and is curated in the `diagnosis` section as well.
Recurrence. p.R67C has been found homozygously in unrelated patients of British origin with no known relationship, which the reporting authors read as a possible founder effect rather than a mutational hotspot.

evidence.snippet: The human RFT1 protein shares 22% identity with its yeast ortholog, which is involved in the translocation of DolPP-GlcNAc(2)Man(5) from the cytosolic into the lumenal side of the endoplasmic reticulum.
evidence.explanation: States the translocation role attributed to the yeast orthologue and carried over to human RFT1.

evidence.snippet: The definition of the RFT1 defect establishes the functional conservation of the DolPP-GlcNAc(2)Man(5) translocation process in eukaryotes.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of the defect as one of a conserved translocation process.

hypotheses/0.description: The original and still most widely cited reading is that RFT1 is itself the transporter that flips Man5GlcNAc2-PP-dolichol from the cytosolic to the luminal leaflet of the ER membrane. On this model the accumulating Man5 intermediate in patient cells is the direct substrate of a missing transport activity, and RFT1-CDG is a transporter deficiency.

evidence.snippet: However, other studies indicated that Rft1 is not required for heptasaccharide lipid flipping in microsomes or unilamellar vesicles reconstituted with ER membrane proteins, nor is it required for the viability of at least one eukaryote.
evidence.explanation: The direct experimental challenge to the flippase attribution.

evidence.snippet: It is therefore not known what essential role Rft1 plays in N-glycosylation.
evidence.explanation: States plainly that the molecular function remains unresolved, which is why this entry curates two hypotheses rather than one mechanism.

evidence.snippet: However, recent evidence suggests that the RFT1 protein would not be the flippase enzyme itself, but would play a critical accessory role in translocating Man5GlcNAc2PP-dolichol to the ER lumen
evidence.explanation: Worth recording because of its date: this 2009 clinical series already stated the accessory-role reading, fifteen years before the 2024 reconstitution work that is the primary support for this hypothesis. The alternative is therefore long-standing rather than a recent reinterpretation.

hypotheses/1.description: Reconstitution work argues against RFT1 being the flippase itself: heptasaccharide lipid flipping proceeds in microsomes and in proteoliposomes reconstituted from ER membrane proteins without a requirement for RFT1, and at least one eukaryote does not need RFT1 for viability. On this reading RFT1 is genuinely essential for N-glycosylation in yeast and mammalian cells, and RFT1-CDG alleles are genuinely damaging, but the molecular activity being lost is something other than direct transbilayer transport — and has not yet been identified.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the central unresolved question of the disease and the reason this entry curates two mechanistic hypotheses rather than one chain. The flippase attribution is inherited from yeast genetics and from the shape of the patient biochemistry: the Man5 intermediate accumulates and the cytosolic free oligosaccharide is absent, exactly as a transport block would predict. But flipping proceeds without RFT1 in microsomes and in reconstituted proteoliposomes, and at least one eukaryote does not require RFT1 for viability. Both observations can be true — RFT1 may be a regulator, assembly factor, or accessory subunit whose loss disables a transport step catalysed by something else. The gap matters for curation because it sets how strongly a downstream causal edge may be stated, and it matters clinically because a transporter deficiency and a regulatory-factor deficiency imply different therapeutic entry points.

open_questions/1.rationale: The published RFT1-CDG cohort is very small and was ascertained through severe presentations — early-onset drug-resistant epilepsy with deafness. In several other CDG (DPM2-CDG among them) an initially uniformly severe phenotype broadened once milder, later-diagnosed patients were found, sometimes surviving to adulthood. Whether RFT1-CDG has a comparable mild tail is unknown, and ascertainment through epileptic encephalopathy would systematically miss it. Deafness may be the more sensitive handle: it is the feature that is consistent across the cohort, and screening syndromic congenital hearing loss for CDG is the route by which a milder tail would most plausibly be found.

open_questions/2.rationale: These three phenotypes are deliberately left without causal edges. The neurological and sensory manifestations are curated as manifestations of the multisystem disease because the literature explicitly frames RFT1-CDG that way ("mainly a neurological disorder", deafness "as part of a severe neurological syndrome"), and the coagulation and prenatal-growth edges rest on stated causal claims. For dysmorphism, cryptorchidism, and hepatomegaly no RFT1-CDG source offers even a disease-level causal statement — they are reported as bare observations, in single patients or small subsets, and hepatomegaly coexisted with repeatedly normal liver function in the series that examined it. Dysmorphism and visceral involvement recur across the CDG group, so a shared glycoprotein-dependent developmental mechanism is plausible, but which target proteins mediate it is unknown, and drawing an edge would manufacture precision the sources do not contain.

evidence.snippet: Viral transmission occurs mainly via animal bite, and once the virus is deposited in peripheral wounds
evidence.explanation: Establishes deposition of virus in peripheral wound tissue as the initiating event.

steps/0.description: A bite from an infected animal deposits saliva-borne lyssavirus into peripheral wound tissue. Virus may replicate locally in muscle or persist at the inoculation site before entering the nervous system, which accounts for the characteristically long and variable incubation period.

evidence.snippet: Texas Red-labeled alpha-bungarotoxin, which binds to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, colocalized precisely with virus at the densities identifying these regions as neuromuscular junctions.
evidence.explanation: Shows virus colocalising with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction.

evidence.snippet: The p75 Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) receptor (p75NTR) binds RABV Glycoprotein (RABV-G) with high affinity.
evidence.explanation: Documents the high-affinity glycoprotein-p75NTR interaction used for neuronal entry.

evidence.snippet: The virus first infects peripheral motor neurons, and symptoms occur after the virus reaches the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Confirms peripheral motor neurons as the first infected cell population in human disease.

steps/1.description: Virions concentrate at the neuromuscular junction, colocalising with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, and are taken up into endosomal compartments of the motor nerve terminal. Rabies virus glycoprotein also binds the p75 neurotrophin receptor with high affinity, giving the virus more than one route into the neuron.

evidence.snippet: Rabies virus (RABV) is a neurotropic virus that depends on long distance axonal transport in order to reach the central nervous system (CNS).
evidence.explanation: States the dependence of CNS invasion on long-distance axonal transport.

evidence.snippet: Hence, RABV may employ p75NTR-dependent transport as a fast mechanism to facilitate movement to the CNS.
evidence.explanation: Supports p75NTR-dependent transport as an accelerated route to the CNS.

evidence.snippet: once the virus is deposited in peripheral wounds, centripetal passage occurs towards the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Describes centripetal spread to the CNS in the clinical review literature.

steps/2.description: Rabies virus depends on long-distance retrograde axonal transport to reach the central nervous system. It travels within acidic compartments largely together with p75NTR, and moves faster and more directively than the receptor's endogenous cargo, indicating that the virus does not merely hitchhike on the transport machinery but manipulates it.

evidence.snippet: Light microscopy showed multifocal mononuclear inflammatory cell infiltrates in the sensory ganglia and a spectrum of degenerative neuronal changes.
evidence.explanation: Documents degenerative change in sensory ganglia in the mouse model.

evidence.snippet: Hence, gangliocytes exhibit selective vulnerability in this animal model.
evidence.explanation: States the selective vulnerability finding, explicitly scoped to the animal model.

evidence.snippet: Local neurological symptoms are likely to be due to RABV infection in local peripheral sensory ganglia
evidence.explanation: Human clinical review attributing bite-site sensory symptoms to local sensory ganglion infection.

steps/3.description: In experimentally infected mice, sensory ganglion neurons show inflammatory infiltrates and degenerative change while CNS neurons remain comparatively spared. This selective peripheral sensory vulnerability is a plausible correlate of the pain, itch, and paresthesias patients report at the healed bite. Clinical review independently attributes those local symptoms to infection of the local peripheral sensory ganglia, so the human correlate is asserted in the clinical literature even though the cellular vulnerability itself is characterised only in mice.

evidence.snippet: The virus first infects peripheral motor neurons, and symptoms occur after the virus reaches the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Establishes CNS arrival as the trigger for clinical disease.

evidence.snippet: Abnormal hypersignal T2 changes were found at hippocampus, hypothalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord of paralytic dogs.
evidence.explanation: Naturally infected dogs show CNS involvement of hippocampus, hypothalamus, brainstem, and spinal cord.

steps/4.description: Virus reaching the spinal cord and brain infects neurons and spreads trans-synaptically through the neuraxis, including brainstem, limbic, and hypothalamic structures. Symptoms begin only after the CNS is reached, which is why the disease is clinically silent throughout the incubation period.

evidence.snippet: Significantly, short-term RNA labeling in the presence of BrUTP strongly suggests that the NBLs are the sites where viral transcription and replication take place.
evidence.explanation: Direct experimental evidence that Negri body-like structures are the sites of viral RNA synthesis.

evidence.snippet: NBs are cytoplasmic inclusion bodies in which viral RNAs (mRNAs as well as genomic and antigenomic RNAs) are synthesized.
evidence.explanation: Characterises Negri bodies as the cytoplasmic compartments of viral RNA synthesis.

evidence.snippet: The co-expression of rabies virus nucleoprotein N and phosphoprotein P is sufficient to induce the formation of cytoplasmic inclusions recapitulating NBs properties.
evidence.explanation: Identifies N and P as the minimal viral components sufficient to build the replication compartment.

steps/5.description: Rabies virus nucleoprotein N and phosphoprotein P condense into spherical, liquid-like cytoplasmic inclusions, the Negri bodies, which act as viral factories. All viral RNA species (genome, antigenome, and mRNAs) are found inside them, and these are the sites where viral transcription and replication occur. Negri bodies are the classical histopathological hallmark of rabies.

evidence.snippet: We propose that altered mitochondrial bioenergetics and cristae architecture probably induce mitophagy, leading to autophagy and consequent neuronal dysfunction in rabies.
evidence.explanation: Proposes the mitochondrial-mitophagy route to neuronal dysfunction; framed as a proposal by the authors, hence PROVISIONAL confidence.

steps/6.description: In naturally infected human and canine brain, respiratory complex activities rise but ATP production does not, consistent with a fall in mitochondrial membrane potential. Disrupted cristae architecture and markers of mitophagy and autophagy accompany these changes, offering one candidate route from infection to neuronal dysfunction in the near absence of cell death.

evidence.snippet: Because morphologic changes in natural rabies are usually relatively mild, it is thought that the severe clinical disease with a fatal outcome must be due to neuronal dysfunction of rabies virus-infected neurons.
evidence.explanation: States the dysfunction-not-destruction principle directly.

evidence.snippet: The presence of minimal neuropathological changes observed in rabies indicates that neuronal dysfunction, rather than neuronal death contributes to the fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: Independent confirmation in naturally infected human and canine brain.

steps/7.description: The defining paradox of rabies neuropathology: clinical disease is catastrophic while morphological changes in the brain are mild. Neurons are largely structurally preserved and inflammation is minimal, so the fatal outcome is attributed to functional impairment of infected neurons rather than to their destruction. The precise basis of that impairment remains unknown.

evidence.snippet: Rabies is an acute, progressive, incurable viral encephalitis.
evidence.explanation: The abstract defines rabies as an acute, progressive, incurable viral encephalitis.

evidence.snippet: Once clinical disease develops, it is almost certainly fatal.
evidence.explanation: Confirms near-universal fatality once clinical disease is established.

steps/8.description: The clinical expression of CNS infection: an acute, relentlessly progressive encephalomyelitis passing through prodrome, an acute neurological phase, coma, and death. Once it begins it is essentially incurable.

evidence.snippet: Larger quantities of rabies viral RNA were found in the brains of furious than in paralytic dogs.
evidence.explanation: Documents the higher brain viral burden of the furious form in the canine model.

evidence.snippet: Paralytic rabies is characterized by delayed viral neuroinvasion and a more intense inflammation than furious rabies.
evidence.explanation: Contrasts the inflammatory and neuroinvasive profile of the paralytic form.

evidence.snippet: Patients with paralytic rabies had longer survival times than those with encephalitic rabies, and also had shorter incubation periods if they had received postexposure prophylaxis.
evidence.explanation: Human case-series evidence that the two forms differ in survival time.

steps/9.description: Rabies presents as either encephalitic (furious) disease, with agitation, hydrophobia, aerophobia, and autonomic instability, or paralytic (dumb) disease, with ascending flaccid weakness and relatively preserved consciousness. In naturally infected dogs, furious disease carries higher brain viral load with only moderate inflammation, whereas paralytic disease shows delayed neuroinvasion with more intense inflammation, suggesting the host inflammatory response shapes which form develops.

evidence.snippet: RVA was found in nerve plexuses in multiple organs, including the gastrointestinal tract.
evidence.explanation: Postmortem human series demonstrating rabies antigen in extraneural nerve plexuses.

evidence.snippet: Minor salivary glands of the tongue contained RVA and major salivary glands showed RVA in plexuses, but not in either acini or ducts.
evidence.explanation: Localises rabies antigen within salivary tissue, the anatomical basis of saliva-borne transmission.

evidence.snippet: RVA was observed in hair follicles of the skin and rarely in pancreatic islets.
evidence.explanation: Cutaneous nerve involvement underpins antemortem nuchal skin biopsy diagnosis.

evidence.snippet: These findings indicate that centrifugal spread of rabies virus to extraneural organs occurs frequently in human rabies.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that centrifugal extraneural spread is a frequent, not exceptional, feature.

steps/10.description: After CNS infection is established, virus moves outward along peripheral nerves and autonomic plexuses to reach salivary glands, skin, cornea, heart, tongue, larynx, adrenal medulla, and the gastrointestinal tract. Salivary gland involvement loads the saliva with virus and closes the transmission cycle; skin and corneal involvement is what makes antemortem nuchal skin biopsy diagnostically useful.

evidence.snippet: These findings show that in nerve-muscle cocultures, the neuromuscular junction is the major site of entry into neurons.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the neuromuscular junction as the major neuronal entry site in a nerve-muscle coculture model.

edges/0.description: Virus deposited at the wound reaches motor nerve terminals at the neuromuscular junction, the principal portal of entry into the nervous system.

evidence.snippet: Local neurological symptoms are likely to be due to RABV infection in local peripheral sensory ganglia
evidence.explanation: Attributes the human bite-site sensory symptoms to infection of the local peripheral sensory ganglia.

edges/1.description: Virus at the inoculation site also reaches the sensory ganglion serving that dermatome, a separate branch from the motor-neuron route and the likely basis of the local sensory symptoms patients report at the healed bite.

evidence.snippet: The progressive increase of virus and tracers in nerve fibers and nerve cell bodies over time is consistent with retrograde transport of endocytosed virus from the motor nerve terminal.
evidence.explanation: Links endosomal uptake at the terminal to retrograde movement toward the cell body.

edges/2.description: Endocytosed virions in acidified compartments of the nerve terminal are carried centripetally along the axon toward the neuronal cell body.

evidence.snippet: The virus first infects peripheral motor neurons, and symptoms occur after the virus reaches the central nervous system.
evidence.explanation: Links peripheral neuronal infection to subsequent CNS infection and symptom onset.

edges/3.description: Arrival of virus at the neuronal cell body establishes infection in the spinal cord and brain, from which trans-synaptic spread disseminates the infection through the neuraxis.

evidence.snippet: Rabies virus infection induces the formation of cytoplasmic inclusion bodies that resemble Negri bodies found in the cytoplasm of some infected nerve cells.
evidence.explanation: Links neuronal infection to formation of the cytoplasmic inclusions seen in nerve cells.

edges/4.description: Infected neurons assemble cytoplasmic viral factories in which viral RNA synthesis takes place.

evidence.snippet: Morphological analysis showed minimal inflammation with preserved neuronal and disrupted mitochondrial structure in both human and canine brains.
evidence.explanation: Documents disrupted mitochondrial structure in infected human and canine brain tissue.

edges/5.description: Infection of CNS neurons is accompanied by disrupted mitochondrial structure and altered bioenergetics in naturally infected human and canine brain.

evidence.snippet: The precise bases of this functional impairment are unknown, and current knowledge on electro-physiological alterations, effects on ion channels and neurotransmission, and neurotoxicity are reviewed.
evidence.explanation: States explicitly that the mechanistic basis of the functional impairment is not established.

edges/6.description: Productive intraneuronal replication is followed by profound functional impairment of infected neurons, although the molecular steps linking replication to dysfunction remain incompletely defined.

evidence.snippet: The presence of minimal neuropathological changes observed in rabies indicates that neuronal dysfunction, rather than neuronal death contributes to the fatal outcome.
evidence.explanation: Ties minimal structural pathology to dysfunction rather than death as the fatal mechanism.

edges/7.description: Bioenergetic failure and mitophagy are proposed to converge on functional impairment of otherwise structurally preserved neurons.

evidence.snippet: Human rabies is an acute, progressive encephalomyelitis that is nearly always fatal once symptoms begin.
evidence.explanation: Names the resulting clinical syndrome and its outcome.

edges/8.description: Widespread neuronal functional failure manifests as an acute, progressive encephalomyelitis that is nearly always fatal.

evidence.snippet: Furious and paralytic rabies differ in clinical manifestations and survival periods.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the two clinical forms as mechanistically and prognostically distinct.

edges/9.description: The encephalomyelitis expresses itself in two distinguishable clinical forms whose separation tracks with viral burden and host inflammatory response.

evidence.snippet: After the development of the central nervous system infection, there is centrifugal spread of the rabies virus to extraneural (systemic) organs.
evidence.explanation: States the direction and timing of centrifugal spread relative to CNS infection.

edges/10.description: Once CNS infection is established, virus travels back out along nerves to peripheral organs.

evidence.snippet: ACIP recommends that prophylaxis for the prevention of rabies in humans exposed to rabies virus should include prompt and thorough wound cleansing followed by passive rabies immunization with human rabies immune globulin (HRIG) and vaccination with a cell culture rabies vaccine.
evidence.explanation: ACIP places prompt thorough wound cleansing first in the prophylaxis sequence.

treatments/0.description: Immediate and thorough washing of the wound is the first step of post-exposure prophylaxis and mechanically removes virus before it can reach nerve terminals. It is cheap, universally available, and frequently skipped.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Removes or inactivates virus at the inoculation site before neuronal entry can occur.

evidence.snippet: Prophylaxis encompasses thorough wound treatment, vaccine administration, and inoculation of rabies immunoglobulin.
evidence.explanation: The abstract includes rabies immunoglobulin as part of prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: HRIG is administered only once (i.e., at the beginning of antirabies prophylaxis) to previously unvaccinated persons to provide immediate, passive, rabies virus neutralizing antibody coverage until the patient responds to HDCV or PCECV by actively producing antibodies.
evidence.explanation: Specifies the timing, single administration, and bridging rationale for HRIG.

treatments/1.description: Human rabies immune globulin infiltrated into and around the wound provides immediate passive neutralising antibody, covering the interval before the vaccine-induced response develops. It is given once, only to previously unvaccinated people.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Neutralising antibody at the wound site blocks virions before they can engage receptors on the motor nerve terminal.

evidence.snippet: Prophylaxis encompasses thorough wound treatment, vaccine administration, and inoculation of rabies immunoglobulin.
evidence.explanation: The abstract describes vaccine administration for prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: If exposure occurs, timely post-exposure prophylaxis can prevent the progression to clinical disease and involves appropriate wound care, the administration of rabies immunoglobulin and vaccination.
evidence.explanation: States the three components of PEP and their preventive effect.

evidence.snippet: Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) for rabies is widely administered and highly effective.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review confirming PEP effectiveness.

evidence.snippet: Timely and appropriate administration of PEP is crucial to prevent rabies, and although people with high-risk exposures or immunosuppression can develop rabies despite adherence to core practices, this occurrence remains exceedingly rare.
evidence.explanation: Qualifies effectiveness; breakthrough infections occur but are exceedingly rare and usually follow deviations from core practice.

treatments/2.description: A series of cell culture-derived rabies vaccine doses given after exposure. Together with wound care and immunoglobulin, post-exposure prophylaxis is highly effective at preventing progression to clinical disease, but only if given promptly.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Active immunisation raises neutralising antibody during the long incubation period, clearing virus before it completes the journey to the central nervous system.

evidence.snippet: PrEP does not eliminate the need for PEP; however, it does simplify the rabies PEP schedule (i.e., eliminates the need for rabies immunoglobulin and decreases the number of vaccine doses required for PEP).
evidence.explanation: States the role and limits of pre-exposure prophylaxis.

evidence.snippet: Preexposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is available for individuals likely to be exposed to the RABV, such as veterinarians and long-term travelers or residents in endemic countries.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the target populations for PrEP.

treatments/3.description: A vaccine series given before any exposure to people at elevated risk: veterinarians, laboratory workers, and long-term travellers to or residents of endemic areas. It does not remove the need for post-exposure prophylaxis but simplifies it, eliminating the immunoglobulin requirement and reducing the number of vaccine doses.

evidence.snippet: Currently, replacing traditional RIG with emerging mAb or mAb combinations is highly recommended due to the limited supply and potential safety risks of RIG.
evidence.explanation: States the rationale for displacing blood-derived RIG with monoclonal antibody products.

evidence.snippet: RM02 and RM05 were non-competing and non-overlapping mAbs targeting epitopes I and III, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Documents the non-overlapping two-epitope cocktail design that guards against neutralisation escape.

treatments/4.description: Monoclonal antibody preparations are replacing blood-derived rabies immune globulin for the passive-immunisation arm of post-exposure prophylaxis, which matters because RIG is chronically in short supply and carries the safety profile of a pooled human blood product. Because single antibodies select for escape at their own epitope, products are formulated as cocktails of non-competing antibodies binding separate epitopes on the viral glycoprotein.

treatments/4/targets/0.description: Like rabies immune globulin, neutralising monoclonal antibody at the wound site blocks virions before they engage receptors on the motor nerve terminal; it is the same mechanistic slot, filled by a recombinant product.

evidence.snippet: Preventing rabies is crucial, as treatment options after symptoms appear are mostly limited to palliative care.
evidence.explanation: States that post-symptomatic management is essentially palliative.

treatments/5.description: Once symptoms begin there is no established curative therapy, and management centres on relieving pain, agitation, and distress. In much of the world patients die at home without access to even this.

evidence.snippet: Over the past 2 decades, no subsequent detailed reports have documented evidence of efficacy. There have been at least 64 cases with failure of the protocol.
evidence.explanation: Documents the absence of efficacy evidence and the accumulated failures.

evidence.snippet: The time has now come to abandon the failed Milwaukee protocol for the therapy of rabies and consider new approaches based our current knowledge of rabies pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Explicit recommendation to abandon the protocol.

evidence.snippet: The Milwaukee protocol, which included therapeutic coma and the administration of ketamine, ribavirin and amantadine, has proved to be ineffective and should no longer be used
evidence.explanation: Independent review naming all three agents and stating the protocol is ineffective and should not be used.

treatments/6.description: An aggressive regimen of therapeutic (induced) coma with ketamine, ribavirin, and amantadine, promoted after a 2004 survival in Milwaukee. It is recorded here as a refuted intervention: two decades produced no documented evidence of efficacy and at least 64 failures, and the current recommendation is to abandon it. Any benefit historically attributed to the protocol is more plausibly explained by the intensive care that accompanied it.

evidence.snippet: The precise bases of this functional impairment are unknown, and current knowledge on electro-physiological alterations, effects on ion channels and neurotransmission, and neurotoxicity are reviewed.
evidence.explanation: States directly that the basis of the functional impairment is unknown, which is the gap this discussion records.

open_questions/0.rationale: This is the central unresolved question of the entry and the reason no post-symptomatic therapy has ever worked. Every candidate mechanism proposed so far - electrophysiological alterations, ion channel and neurotransmission effects, neurotoxicity, and more recently mitochondrial bioenergetic failure with mitophagy - remains a candidate rather than a demonstrated cause. Until the effector step is identified there is no rational target for therapy after symptom onset, which is precisely the window in which every attempted treatment, the Milwaukee protocol included, has failed.

evidence.snippet: Raynaud's phenomenon is a peripheral vascular disorder characterized by exaggerated vasoconstrictive response to certain stimuli, most typically cold exposure and emotional stress.
evidence.explanation: Cold exposure is the primary trigger for RP attacks.

evidence.snippet: estrogen plays a fundamental role in potentiating the expression and function of α2C adrenoceptor (α2C-AR), the sole mediator of local cooling-induced vasoconstriction
evidence.explanation: Cold exposure activates alpha-2C-AR-mediated vasoconstriction.

evidence.snippet: recurrent episodes of digital vasospasm triggered by exposure to physical/chemical or emotional stress
evidence.explanation: Emotional stress is a recognized trigger alongside physical stimuli.

evidence.snippet: alterations in activity of the peripheral adrenoceptor have been implicated, specifically an enhanced smooth muscle contraction due to overexpression or hyperactivity of postsynaptic alpha 2 receptors
evidence.explanation: Alpha-2 adrenoceptor hyperactivity drives the exaggerated smooth muscle contraction.

evidence.snippet: estrogen plays a fundamental role in potentiating the expression and function of α2C adrenoceptor (α2C-AR), the sole mediator of local cooling-induced vasoconstriction
evidence.explanation: Identifies alpha-2C-AR as the sole mediator of cold-induced vasospasm.

steps/2.description: Cold triggers alpha-2C adrenoceptor (ADRA2C) activation in microvascular smooth muscle cells, mediating local cooling-induced vasoconstriction of digital arteries and arterioles. Alpha-2C-AR is the sole mediator of cold-induced vasoconstriction in the peripheral vasculature.

evidence.snippet: Endothelial damage and activation occur early, possibly triggered by various infectious agents and autoantibodies. Endothelial dysfunction, along with defects in endothelial progenitor cells, leads to defective angiogenesis and vasculogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Endothelial dysfunction is an early event driving vascular pathology.

evidence.snippet: once damaged, endothelial cells can be dysfunctionally activated, thus becoming unable to undergo angiogenesis and promoting perivascular inflammation. They can also undergo apoptosis, transdifferentiate into profibrotic myofibroblasts
evidence.explanation: Describes mechanisms of endothelial dysfunction including EndoMT and failed angiogenesis in SSc-associated RP.

steps/3.description: Impaired endothelium-dependent vasodilation with reduced nitric oxide (NO) and prostacyclin bioavailability and increased production of endothelin-1 (ET-1). The imbalance between vasoconstrictors and vasodilators favors persistent vasoconstriction, platelet activation, and intimal proliferation. In secondary RP associated with systemic sclerosis, endothelial damage leads to defective angiogenesis, endothelial-to-mesenchymal transition, and progressive capillary loss.

evidence.snippet: The pathogenesis of RP involves a complex interaction between the vascular wall, nerves, hormones, and humoral factors, disrupting the balance between vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
evidence.explanation: Neurovascular dysregulation as a central mechanism.

steps/4.description: Increased sympathetic adrenergic control of digital resistance vessels contributes to exaggerated cold-induced vasoconstriction. The pathogenesis involves a complex interaction between the vascular wall, nerves, hormones, and humoral factors disrupting the balance between vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

evidence.snippet: A significant enrichment by gene ontology enrichment analysis was detected in a subset of genes involved in biological processes including cellular response to luteinizing hormone stimulus, negative regulation of fibrinolysis, negative regulation of smooth muscle cell apoptotic process, plasminogen activation
evidence.explanation: GO analysis of RP-associated genes shows enrichment in coagulation/fibrinolysis pathways relevant to intravascular abnormalities.

evidence.snippet: Through the use of KEGG pathways, we were able to identify many molecular processes that contribute to RP, including the AGE-RAGE signaling pathway in diabetic complications, complement and coagulation cascades, fluid shear stress, atherosclerosis.
evidence.explanation: KEGG analysis confirms complement/coagulation cascade involvement in RP.

steps/5.description: Platelet activation and release of thromboxane A2 and serotonin contribute to vasospasm. Altered coagulation and fibrinolysis pathways and increased blood viscosity further impair microvascular flow during episodes. Gene ontology analysis identifies enrichment in negative regulation of fibrinolysis and complement/coagulation cascades among RP-associated genes.

evidence.snippet: Raynaud's phenomenon (RP) is a condition characterized by episodic, excessive vasoconstriction in the fingers and toes, triggered by cold or stress.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the core vasospastic mechanism that RhoA/ROCK potentiates.

steps/6.description: RhoA/ROCK signaling potentiates alpha-2C adrenoceptor-mediated vasoconstriction and reactive oxygen species generation in vascular smooth muscle cells, amplifying the vasospastic response to cold.

evidence.snippet: Raynaud's phenomenon incidence is significantly higher in premenopausal females compared to age-matched males, highlighting a role of the female hormone, estrogen, in Raynaud's phenomenon pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Estrogen potentiates alpha-2C-AR, explaining sex-based differences in RP incidence.

steps/7.description: Estrogen potentiates alpha-2C adrenoceptor expression and function, contributing to the significantly higher incidence of Raynaud phenomenon in premenopausal females compared to age-matched males.

evidence.snippet: recent advances in our understanding of the pathophysiology have highlighted novel potential therapeutic targets
evidence.explanation: Prete et al. review discusses pathogenic mechanisms including oxidative stress in RP pathophysiology.

steps/8.description: Recurrent vasospastic episodes cause ischemia-reperfusion injury with generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and endothelial damage. ROS-dependent signaling also regulates alpha-2C-AR expression and translocation in vascular smooth muscle cells, creating a feed-forward loop of vascular dysfunction.

edges/0.description: Alpha-2C-AR activation is potentiated by RhoA/ROCK signaling.

evidence.snippet: estrogen plays a fundamental role in potentiating the expression and function of α2C adrenoceptor (α2C-AR), the sole mediator of local cooling-induced vasoconstriction
evidence.explanation: Names alpha-2C adrenoceptor as the sole mediator of local cooling-induced vasoconstriction, which is this node's content and names the exposure that drives it.

evidence.snippet: Raynaud's phenomenon is a peripheral vascular disorder characterized by exaggerated vasoconstrictive response to certain stimuli, most typically cold exposure and emotional stress.
evidence.explanation: Characterises the disorder as an exaggerated vasoconstrictive response to stimuli, most typically cold. It supports cold as the usual trigger of the response, but it is a definition of the disorder rather than a finding about this receptor, which is why it is partial while the same paper's mechanistic sentence above is not.

edges/1.description: The closest exposure-to-node fit in this tranche: the node is named for cold-induced vasoconstriction, and the first item names the receptor as the sole mediator of local cooling-induced vasoconstriction. Exposure and mechanism are in the same clause, which is why this one is direct where the others are not. Direct is recorded knowing that cold reaches the receptor through mitochondrial reactive oxygen species and RhoA/ROCK, which this entry models as a separate node: those steps sit inside the cold-induced vasoconstriction this node is named for rather than on the edge into it, so they are internal to the target and not intermediates the edge steps over. Noted so the question is not reopened later.

evidence.snippet: recurrent episodes of digital vasospasm triggered by exposure to physical/chemical or emotional stress
evidence.explanation: Names emotional stress among the triggers of recurrent digital vasospasm. It reaches the spasm at the end of the chain rather than the sympathetic step this link targets, so it supports the longer path through this node without isolating it.

edges/2.description: Pointed at sympathetic dysregulation rather than at the cold-receptor node, because that is the route this entry gives a stressor that is not cold, and the node's own description places increased sympathetic adrenergic control on the digital resistance vessels. The intermediates are recorded as known on the strength of that mapped route rather than of the quoted sentence, which stops at the vasospasm and does not name the nerves.

evidence.snippet: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (CCBs), such as nifedipine, are commonly used for vasodilation.
evidence.explanation: CCBs are established first-line pharmacotherapy for RP.

evidence.snippet: CCBs (especially the dihydropyridine class) may be useful in reducing the frequency, duration, severity of attacks, pain and disability associated with Raynaud's phenomenon.
evidence.explanation: Cochrane systematic review of 38 RCTs demonstrating CCBs reduce attack frequency and severity.

treatments/0.description: Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine, amlodipine) are first-line pharmacotherapy. They reduce frequency and severity of vasospastic attacks by inhibiting calcium influx into vascular smooth muscle cells.

evidence.snippet: Most patients with RS can be managed conservatively, with avoidance of cold exposure or hand warming.
evidence.explanation: Conservative management with cold avoidance is first-line for most patients.

treatments/1.description: Behavioral modification including wearing warm gloves, avoiding cold exposure, and using hand warmers. First-line non-pharmacological management for all patients with Raynaud phenomenon.

evidence.snippet: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and prostaglandin analogs are alternative options for patients who do not respond to CCBs or have ischemic tissue damage.
evidence.explanation: PDE5 inhibitors are second-line options for refractory RP.

evidence.snippet: Sildenafil improved digital blood flow and RP symptoms in SSc patients after 8 weeks of treatment, and might be a good therapeutic option for secondary RP.
evidence.explanation: RCT demonstrating sildenafil improves microvascular blood flow in SSc-associated RP.

treatments/2.description: Sildenafil and tadalafil improve digital blood flow by inhibiting PDE5, increasing cGMP levels, and enhancing nitric oxide-mediated vasodilation. Used as second-line therapy for refractory cases or when CCBs are insufficient.

evidence.snippet: Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors and prostaglandin analogs are alternative options for patients who do not respond to CCBs or have ischemic tissue damage.
evidence.explanation: Prostacyclin analogs are alternative options for severe/refractory RP.

treatments/3.description: Intravenous iloprost is used for severe Raynaud phenomenon with digital ischemia or ulceration. Provides potent vasodilation and antiplatelet effects.

evidence.snippet: Bosentan, an endothelin-1 receptor antagonist, has shown effectiveness in treating and preventing digital ulcers, especially in patients with multiple ulcers.
evidence.explanation: Bosentan is effective for digital ulcer prevention in SSc-associated RP.

treatments/4.description: Bosentan blocks endothelin-1 receptor signaling and has shown effectiveness in treating and preventing digital ulcers, especially in patients with systemic sclerosis-associated Raynaud phenomenon with multiple ulcers.

evidence.snippet: sympathectomy surgery can be used to control RP symptoms. However, botulinum toxin injections require repeated administration, and sympathectomy's long-term effectiveness is uncertain.
evidence.explanation: Sympathectomy is an option for severe cases but has uncertain long-term efficacy.

treatments/5.description: Surgical sympathectomy can be used for severe, refractory Raynaud phenomenon to reduce sympathetic vasoconstriction. Long-term effectiveness is uncertain.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 4 (MC4DN4) is a form of COX deficiency associated with pathogenic variants in the SCO1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Confirms SCO1 variants cause MC4DN4, a nuclear copper-delivery COX deficiency.

steps/1.description: Biallelic SCO1 variants impair copper delivery to the COX CuA center, preventing assembly of a functional Complex IV holoenzyme.

evidence.snippet: Mammalian cytochrome c oxidase (COX) catalyses the transfer of reducing equivalents from cytochrome c to molecular oxygen and pumps protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane.
evidence.explanation: Defines the terminal electron-transfer and proton-pumping function lost in SCO1-related COX deficiency.

steps/2.description: Loss of functional COX blocks electron transfer from cytochrome c to oxygen and proton pumping, collapsing oxidative ATP synthesis, with prominent hepatic and neurologic involvement.

evidence.snippet: neonatal-onset hepatic failure and encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: The report describes SCO1 mutations in COX deficiency presenting with neonatal-onset hepatic failure.

steps/3.description: Neonatal-onset hepatic failure, a classic feature of SCO1-related COX deficiency.

evidence.snippet: neonatal-onset hepatic failure and encephalopathy
evidence.explanation: Encephalopathy is a core feature of SCO1-related COX deficiency.

steps/4.description: Encephalopathy, including developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in the expanded spectrum.

evidence.snippet: We describe three patients with MC4DN4 with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), hypopituitarism, and SCO1 pathogenic variants.
evidence.explanation: Documents developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in SCO1/MC4DN4.

steps/5.description: Epileptic seizures in the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype.

evidence.snippet: We describe three patients with MC4DN4 with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), hypopituitarism, and SCO1 pathogenic variants.
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive hypopituitarism in the expanded SCO1/MC4DN4 phenotype.

steps/6.description: Progressive hypopituitarism, an expansion of the SCO1/MC4DN4 phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Human diseases associated with COX deficiency including encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, and fatal lactic acidosis are caused by mutations in COX subunits or assembly factors.
evidence.explanation: Lactic acidosis is a recognized manifestation of COX deficiency.

steps/7.description: Elevated lactate from impaired oxidative metabolism.

evidence.snippet: This proline, adjacent to the CxxxC copper-binding domain of SCO1, is likely to play a crucial role in the tridimentional structure of the domain.
evidence.explanation: Locates the pathogenic SCO1 missense change in the copper-binding domain, tying loss of copper delivery to the resulting isolated COX deficiency.

edges/1.description: Failure of CuA assembly yields a catalytically inactive enzyme.

edges/2.description: Energy failure in hepatocytes drives neonatal hepatic failure. Note that the PMID:11013136 abstract states the hepatic presentation only in its title, so no exact-quote snippet from the cached abstract supports this edge; evidence is deliberately omitted rather than sourced from a title.

evidence.snippet: We describe three patients with MC4DN4 with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE), hypopituitarism, and SCO1 pathogenic variants.
evidence.explanation: Reports encephalopathy in three genetically confirmed MC4DN4 patients, downstream of the SCO1 Complex IV defect.

edges/3.description: Energy deficit in the CNS produces encephalopathy.

evidence.snippet: Our findings expand knowledge of phenotypic variability in MC4DN4 and suggest that SCO1 is a candidate gene for genetic hypopituitarism and DEE.
evidence.explanation: Names SCO1 as a candidate gene for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, supporting the edge to seizures.

edges/4.description: CNS energy failure in the developmental and epileptic encephalopathy phenotype contributes to seizures.

evidence.snippet: Pituitary deficiency in these patients progressively worsened and mainly involved growth hormone secretion and thyroid function.
evidence.explanation: Documents progressive pituitary failure in MC4DN4 patients, supporting the hypothalamic-pituitary arm of the multisystem energy failure.

edges/5.description: Multisystem mitochondrial energy failure can involve the hypothalamic-pituitary axis, producing hypopituitarism.

evidence.snippet: Human diseases associated with COX deficiency including encephalomyopathies, Leigh syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathies, and fatal lactic acidosis are caused by mutations in COX subunits or assembly factors.
evidence.explanation: Review places lactic acidosis downstream of COX deficiency caused by assembly-factor mutations, the lesion class SCO1 belongs to.

edges/6.description: Impaired oxidative phosphorylation shifts pyruvate metabolism toward lactate accumulation, producing lactic acidosis.

evidence.snippet: Mitochondrial complex IV deficiency nuclear type 4 (MC4DN4) is a form of COX deficiency associated with pathogenic variants in the SCO1 gene.
evidence.explanation: Identifies SCO1 as the causal gene for MC4DN4.

treatments/0.description: No curative therapy; supportive management of hepatic failure, seizures, endocrine deficits, and lactic acidosis.

evidence.snippet: The ribosome is one of the main antibiotic targets in the bacterial cell.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the bacterial ribosome as the lincosamide/macrolide target, the step this node represents. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review.

steps/0.description: Streptococcus pyogenes depends on 70S-ribosome translation. For patients with immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity, clindamycin (a lincosamide) and macrolides bind the 50S subunit and arrest bacterial protein synthesis — a ribosomal target distinct from the PBP target of the first-line beta-lactams.

evidence.snippet: clindamycin has great efficacy against the production of bacterial exoproteins
evidence.explanation: Study of Streptococcus pyogenes exoprotein production confirming that the protein-synthesis inhibitor clindamycin suppresses bacterial exoprotein (toxin) synthesis. Evidence source is IN_VITRO (bacterial culture/exoprotein assay).

steps/1.description: The scarlet fever rash is driven by streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins (SPEs) — secreted superantigen proteins. Because these toxins are translated products, a protein-synthesis inhibitor such as clindamycin suppresses their production independently of bacterial killing. This anti-toxin rationale is the principal reason clindamycin is valued in toxin-mediated and invasive group A streptococcal disease, beyond its role as a penicillin-allergy alternative.

evidence.snippet: Group A ß-hemolytic Streptococcus (GABHS) is the leading bacterial cause of acute pharyngitis in children and adolescents worldwide.
evidence.explanation: This supports the upper-airway streptococcal infection node underlying scarlet fever.

steps/2.description: Streptococcus pyogenes colonizes and infects the upper respiratory tract, producing acute pharyngitis with fever and systemic inflammatory symptoms.

evidence.snippet: The early diagnosis and treatment of this disease is critical to obviate the development of local and systemic sequelae such as acute rheumatic fever, endocarditis, and glomerulonephritis.
evidence.explanation: This supports downstream post-streptococcal sequelae as clinically important complications of scarlet fever.

steps/3.description: Scarlet fever can be followed by clinically important local and systemic sequelae, including acute rheumatic fever, endocarditis, and glomerulonephritis, which motivates early diagnosis and treatment.

evidence.snippet: Sixteen emm types were identified with predominance of emm12 (66.4%) and emm1 (29.8%).
evidence.explanation: This supports emm-type predominance among GAS isolates from children with scarlet fever in Shanghai.

evidence.snippet: Four novel M1UK isolates were found in Shanghai, with distinctive characteristics of presence of speC and ssa.
evidence.explanation: This supports emergence of M1UK isolates carrying scarlet-fever-relevant superantigen genes.

steps/4.description: Recent scarlet fever and GAS surveillance has identified changing emm-type distributions, including emm12, emm1, and M1UK lineages with distinctive superantigen gene profiles.

evidence.snippet: Superantigens (SAgs) secreted by this Group A streptococcus (GAS) usually overstimulate the human immune system, causing an amplified hypersensitivity reaction leading to initial symptoms such as sore throat, high fever, and a sandpaper-like skin rash.
evidence.explanation: This directly connects GAS superantigens to immune overactivation and classic scarlet fever symptoms.

evidence.snippet: GAS promotes severe inflammation through mechanisms involving inflammasomes, IL-1β, and T-cell hyperactivation.
evidence.explanation: This supports inflammatory and T-cell activation mechanisms for GAS pathogenicity.

steps/5.description: Streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins act as superantigens and trigger immune activation, producing the characteristic scarlatiniform rash and mucosal findings of scarlet fever.

evidence.snippet: although glycan chain polymerization occurs in the absence of transpeptidation (for example, in the presence of penicillin), efficient transpeptidation requires ongoing GTase reactions
evidence.explanation: Establishes that beta-lactams (penicillin) act by blocking PBP transpeptidation, the cross-linking step this node represents. Evidence source is OTHER as this is a review article.

steps/6.description: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus) builds and maintains its peptidoglycan cell wall by penicillin-binding protein (PBP) transpeptidase cross-linking. This essential, bacteria-specific reaction is the target of the penicillin and amoxicillin used to treat scarlet fever; beta-lactam acylation of the PBP active site halts cross-linking and is bactericidal. Group A Streptococcus has retained universal penicillin susceptibility, which is why beta-lactams remain unconditionally first-line.

evidence.snippet: Superantigens (SAgs) secreted by this Group A streptococcus (GAS) usually overstimulate the human immune system, causing an amplified hypersensitivity reaction leading to initial symptoms such as sore throat, high fever, and a sandpaper-like skin rash.
evidence.explanation: This directly supports the rash phenotype and connects it to GAS superantigens.

steps/7.description: A diffuse erythematous scarlatiniform rash is the defining rash phenotype.

edges/0.description: Toxigenic strains can produce superantigenic exotoxins that drive the scarlet fever rash.

edges/1.description: Untreated or delayed treatment of scarlet fever can permit local and systemic sequelae.

edges/2.description: Toxin-mediated immune activation produces the diffuse erythematous rash.

edges/3.description: Toxigenic emm lineages contribute superantigen profiles that feed the toxin-mediated scarlet fever mechanism.

evidence.snippet: Antimicrobial therapy should be initiated without delay once the diagnosis is confirmed. Oral penicillin V and amoxicillin remain the drugs of choice.
evidence.explanation: This supports prompt beta-lactam therapy as first-line management for confirmed GAS pharyngitis/scarlet fever.

evidence.snippet: Antibiotics should be prescribed early to mitigate its duration, sequelae, and community spread.
evidence.explanation: This supports early antibiotic treatment to reduce disease duration, complications, and transmission.

treatments/0.description: Penicillin or amoxicillin therapy treats group A streptococcal infection, reduces symptom duration, and helps prevent immune-mediated complications.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Penicillin and amoxicillin acylate the streptococcal PBP transpeptidase, blocking peptidoglycan cross-linking and killing group A Streptococcus.

evidence.snippet: For patients who have a non-anaphylactic allergy to penicillin, oral cephalosporin is an acceptable alternative. For patients with a history of immediate, anaphylactic-type hypersensitivity to penicillin, oral clindamycin, clarithromycin, and azithromycin are acceptable alternatives.
evidence.explanation: This supports cephalosporin and clindamycin-containing alternatives for patients with penicillin allergy.

treatments/1.description: Cephalosporins can be used for non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy, while clindamycin and macrolides are alternatives for immediate-type penicillin hypersensitivity.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Clindamycin and macrolides bind the 50S ribosome and arrest streptococcal protein synthesis in penicillin-allergic patients.

treatments/1/targets/1.description: Clindamycin suppresses production of the streptococcal pyrogenic exotoxins that drive the scarlet fever rash, independently of bacterial killing.

evidence.snippet: Sequencing of genes in our interval led to the identification of five putative causal mutations in gene UBIAD1, in our family as well as in four other small families of various geographic origins.
evidence.explanation: One of the two 2007 studies that established UBIAD1 as the SCD gene.

evidence.snippet: Predictions of the protein structure indicated that a prenyl-transferase domain and several transmembrane helices are affected by these mutations.
evidence.explanation: Localizes SCD variants to the prenyltransferase domain and transmembrane helices.

evidence.snippet: More than 20 UBIAD1 mutations have been found to associate with human SCD.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the breadth of the SCD-associated allelic series.

steps/1.description: A heterozygous missense variant in UBIAD1 (1p36.22) substitutes a highly conserved residue in the prenyltransferase domain or an adjacent transmembrane helix. Over 20 SCD-associated UBIAD1 variants are known; p.Asn102Ser is a recurrent hotspot found in unrelated families of both European and Asian ancestry. The variants act by conferring an abnormal, persistent interaction with HMG-CoA reductase rather than by simple loss of catalytic activity.

evidence.snippet: Mutant forms of UBIAD1 associated with Schnyder corneal dystrophy (SCD), a human eye disease characterized by corneal accumulation of cholesterol, are sequestered in the ER and block reductase degradation.
evidence.explanation: Establishes ER sequestration of SCD-mutant UBIAD1 and its coupling to blocked reductase degradation.

evidence.snippet: Results of this characterization support a model in which UBIAD1 continuously cycles between the ER and medial-trans Golgi of isoprenoid-replete cells.
evidence.explanation: Describes the normal GGpp-regulated ER-Golgi cycling that the SCD variant disrupts.

evidence.snippet: Sequestration in the ER protects SCD-associated UBIAD1 from autophagy and allows intracellular accumulation of the mutant protein, which amplifies the inhibitory effect on reductase ERAD.
evidence.explanation: Shows ER sequestration is self-amplifying by protecting the mutant protein from autophagic clearance.

steps/2.description: Wild-type UBIAD1 cycles between the ER and the medial-trans Golgi, with GGpp abundance acting as the switch: when GGpp is plentiful UBIAD1 is released from HMGCR and moves to the Golgi, and when GGpp falls UBIAD1 is trapped in the ER. SCD-associated UBIAD1 is constitutively trapped in the ER regardless of GGpp, mislocalizing the protein to the compartment where HMGCR resides. ER sequestration additionally shields the mutant protein from autophagy-mediated degradation, so it accumulates intracellularly and amplifies its own downstream effect.

evidence.snippet: SCD-associated mutations in UBIAD1 block its displacement from reductase in the presence of geranylgeraniol, thereby preventing degradation of reductase.
evidence.explanation: Identifies the exact molecular defect, failure of geranylgeraniol-induced displacement from HMGCR.

evidence.snippet: Geranylgeraniol inhibits binding of UBIAD1 to reductase, allowing its degradation and promoting transport of UBIAD1 from the ER to the Golgi.
evidence.explanation: Describes the normal regulatory switch that SCD variants break.

evidence.snippet: We now report knockin mice expressing SCD-associated UBIAD1 accumulate HMGCR in several tissues resulting from ER sequestration of mutant UBIAD1 and inhibition of HMGCR ERAD.
evidence.explanation: In vivo confirmation that the SCD variant blocks HMGCR ERAD and causes HMGCR accumulation.

steps/3.description: HMG-CoA reductase is normally subject to sterol-accelerated, ER-associated degradation, a feedback arm that shuts down the mevalonate pathway when sterols are abundant. Sterols promote UBIAD1-HMGCR binding, which transiently spares the enzyme so that nonsterol isoprenoid synthesis can continue; GGpp then displaces UBIAD1 and permits maximal degradation. SCD-mutant UBIAD1 cannot be displaced, so HMGCR escapes ERAD and accumulates, as demonstrated in cultured cells, in patient-derived material, and in knock-in mice, where HMGCR protein accumulates across several tissues.

evidence.snippet: Our results show that UBIAD1 is a human MK-4 biosynthetic enzyme
evidence.explanation: Establishes the normal enzymatic function of UBIAD1 that SCD variants impair.

evidence.snippet: Our studies revealed that SCD-associated UBIAD1 exhibited reduced MK-4 synthetic activity, which may result from its reduced affinity for GGpp.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies reduced MK-4 synthesis and attributes it to reduced GGpp affinity.

evidence.snippet: Our findings suggest that UBIAD1's MK-4 biosynthetic activity does not directly correlate with the phenotypes of SCD patients.
evidence.explanation: Argues against MK-4 deficiency as the primary driver, which is why this node is curated as an alternative hypothesis rather than the canonical chain.

steps/4.description: UBIAD1 is the human menaquinone-4 (vitamin K2) biosynthetic enzyme, prenylating vitamin K precursors using GGpp. SCD-associated variants have reduced MK-4 synthetic activity, plausibly through reduced GGpp affinity. The contribution of this arm to corneal disease is uncertain and is curated as an alternative rather than the canonical mechanism: SCD patients do not show the phenotypes expected from MK-4 or vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation deficiency, and per-variant MK-4 activity does not track with clinical severity. A vitamin-K readout is nonetheless measurably abnormal in SCD keratocytes and plasma.

evidence.snippet: Although 2/3 of SCD patients also have systemic hypercholesterolemia, the incidence of hypercholesterolemia is also increased in unaffected members of SCD pedigrees. Consequently, SCD is thought to result from a local metabolic defect in the cornea.
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the causative defect is corneal-local, not systemic lipid handling.

evidence.snippet: The heterozygous Ubiad1 G184R knock-in (Ubiad1G184R/+) mice expressed elevated levels of HMGCR protein in various tissues.
evidence.explanation: In vivo evidence that the SCD allele raises HMGCR protein, the driver of increased synthesis.

steps/5.description: Sustained HMGCR activity raises local cholesterol synthesis in corneal cells. Because the defect is intrinsic to the corneal cells themselves rather than to circulating lipoproteins, the resulting sterol excess is corneal even when serum lipids are normal, which is the basis for regarding SCD as a local corneal metabolic defect.

evidence.snippet: Schnyder crystalline corneal dystrophy (SCCD; MIM 121800) is a rare autosomal dominant disease characterized by an abnormal increase in cholesterol and phospholipid deposition in the cornea, leading to progressive corneal opacification.
evidence.explanation: States the defining deposition of cholesterol and phospholipid in the cornea.

evidence.snippet: IVCM revealed hyperreflective deposits in the epithelium and throughout the stroma, thin subepithelial nerves, and needle-shaped and rectangular crystals. Keratocyte nuclei were rare or undetectable.
evidence.explanation: In vivo confocal characterization of the epithelial and stromal deposits and crystal morphology.

steps/6.description: Unesterified cholesterol, cholesterol esters, and phospholipids accumulate in the basal corneal epithelium, Bowman layer, and anterior-to-mid stroma. In roughly half of patients the lipid organizes into needle-shaped, birefringent subepithelial and anterior stromal crystals; in the remainder it produces only diffuse haze. Ultrastructurally the deposits present as multilamellar bodies and, on histology, as vacuolization of basal epithelial cells and empty interlamellar stromal vacuoles where lipid was dissolved out during processing. The corneal endothelium is characteristically spared.

evidence.snippet: The corneal findings in SCD are very predictable depending on the age of the individual, with initial central corneal haze and/or crystals, subsequent appearance of arcus lipoides in the third decade and formation of midperipheral haze in the late fourth decade.
evidence.explanation: Defines the age-staged spatial progression of corneal opacification.

evidence.snippet: Although excellent scotopic vision continues until middle age in SCCD, most patients had PKP by the 7th decade. SCCD causes progressive corneal opacification, which may result in glare and disproportionate loss of photopic vision.
evidence.explanation: Documents the photopic-versus-scotopic dissociation and the surgical endpoint.

steps/7.description: Deposition follows a highly age-predictable spatial sequence: central corneal haze and/or crystals first, arcus lipoides in the third decade, then midperipheral haze in the late fourth decade. The optical consequence is asymmetric across lighting conditions, since scattering degrades bright-light (photopic) vision and produces disabling glare while scotopic acuity is comparatively preserved into middle age. Cumulative opacification drives progressive visual disability and, in most patients, corneal surgery by the seventh decade.

evidence.snippet: SCD-associated UBIAD1 resists GGpp-induced release and is sequestered in ER to inhibit ERAD.
evidence.explanation: Directly links the SCD variant to failed GGpp-triggered release and ER sequestration.

edges/1.description: The missense substitution lowers UBIAD1 affinity for GGpp, so the mutant protein fails to undergo the GGpp-triggered release that normally licenses its exit from the ER.

evidence.snippet: We observed reduced MK-4 synthesis by UBIAD1 altered by SCD mutations p.N102S, p.G177R/E, and p.D112N, and molecular models showed p.G177-mutant UBIAD1 disrupted transmembrane helices and active site residues.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates reduced MK-4 synthetic activity for several SCD variants.

edges/2.description: The same substitutions reduce the enzyme's capacity to prenylate vitamin K to MK-4, in at least some cases through the same reduced GGpp affinity.

evidence.snippet: In contrast to the Golgi localization of wild-type UBIAD1, SCD-associated mutants mainly resided in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and competed with Insig-1 for HMGCR binding, thereby preventing HMGCR from degradation and increasing cholesterol biosynthesis.
evidence.explanation: States the Insig-1 competition step linking ER retention to blocked HMGCR degradation.

edges/3.description: ER-retained mutant UBIAD1 outcompetes Insig-1 for binding to HMGCR, removing the adaptor required to commit HMGCR to ubiquitin-dependent ER-associated degradation.

evidence.snippet: The stabilization of HMGCR by UBIAD1 increases cholesterol biosynthesis and eventually causes cholesterol accumulation in the cornea.
evidence.explanation: States the causal step from HMGCR stabilization to increased cholesterol synthesis.

edges/4.description: Stabilized HMGCR raises flux through the rate-limiting step of the mevalonate pathway, increasing cholesterol synthesis.

evidence.snippet: Impaired MK-4 synthesis is a biochemical defect identified in SCD suggesting UBIAD1 links vitamin K and cholesterol metabolism through physical contact between enzymes and metabolites.
evidence.explanation: Supports a physical link between the vitamin K and cholesterol arms but does not establish the causal intermediates, hence INDIRECT.

edges/5.description: Proposed but unresolved link. UBIAD1 physically contacts both HMGCR and SOAT1, and cholesterol competes with GGpp for the UBIAD1 substrate-binding cleft, suggesting that a defect in the MK-4 arm could perturb corneal cholesterol handling; the intermediates are not established.

evidence.snippet: Corneas from aged knockin mice exhibit signs of opacification and sterol overaccumulation.
evidence.explanation: Shows sterol overaccumulation in the cornea downstream of blocked HMGCR ERAD.

edges/6.description: Excess locally synthesized unesterified cholesterol, together with phospholipid, is deposited in and around corneal cells.

evidence.snippet: These patients often complained of glare preoperatively, which most likely resulted from light scattering from the corneal cholesterol.
evidence.explanation: Attributes the glare symptom to light scattering by the deposited corneal cholesterol.

edges/7.description: Lipid deposits within the normally transparent, regularly ordered corneal stroma disrupt its refractive uniformity and scatter incident light.

evidence.snippet: The results suggest that N102S may be a mutation hot spot because the affected families were unrelated including Caucasian and Asian individuals.
evidence.explanation: Establishes N102S as a recurrent hotspot across ancestries rather than a founder allele.

evidence.snippet: There was no genotype phenotype correlation except for the T175I mutation which demonstrated prominent diffuse corneal haze, typically without corneal crystals.
evidence.explanation: Documents the single recognized genotype-phenotype correlation in SCD.

evidence.snippet: The novel p.Thr120Arg is the fourth SCD-causing variant lying within the FARM motif of the UBIAD1 protein, which underlines a high importance of this motif for SCD pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: Highlights clustering of pathogenic variants within the FARM motif.

evidence.snippet: Our newly reported UBIAD1 mutation suggests that CDCD is actually a variant of SCD.
evidence.explanation: Basis for absorbing central discoid corneal dystrophy into SCD as a synonym rather than a separate entity.

evidence.snippet: After 22 months of follow-up, the best-corrected visual acuity had increased from 0.5 to 0.9 in the right eye and from 0.3 to 0.9 in the left eye.
evidence.explanation: Documents visual gain after deep PTK in an SCD patient.

evidence.snippet: PTK can increase patients' visual acuity and eliminate the need for aggressive management through penetrating keratoplasty or deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty.
evidence.explanation: Supports PTK as a keratoplasty-sparing first-line option.

evidence.snippet: No recurrence was detected after 68 months of follow-up.
evidence.explanation: Indicates durable benefit over almost six years in one reported case.

treatments/0.description: Excimer-laser ablation of the anterior cornea to remove subepithelial and anterior stromal crystals and haze. Often preferred as first-line surgery for visually significant anterior disease because it is tissue-sparing and avoids the graft-related risks of keratoplasty; deep, multizone/multipass techniques extend its reach. The principal limitation is cumulative corneal thinning, which caps the number of feasible retreatments, so preoperative pachymetry is required. It is palliative, not disease-modifying: the underlying UBIAD1 defect persists and deposits can re-form.

evidence.snippet: PTK may be effective in the treatment of SCCD, especially if the crystals are the cause of visual disturbance.
evidence.explanation: Ties the benefit of PTK specifically to removal of the crystalline deposits.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Physically ablates the deposit-laden anterior cornea rather than altering the metabolic defect that generates the deposits.

evidence.snippet: PKP was reported in 20 of 37 (54%) patients > or =50 years and 10 of 13 (77%) of patients > or =70.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the age-dependent likelihood of requiring keratoplasty.

evidence.snippet: In all eyes, no disease recurrence or corneal graft rejection was observed during the follow-up period, and graft transparency was maintained.
evidence.explanation: Long-term graft survival without recurrence in a genotyped SCD pedigree.

treatments/1.description: Full-thickness corneal transplantation, reserved for advanced disease or when PTK is insufficient or precluded by corneal thickness. It is the endpoint for most patients by the seventh decade. Long-term outcomes in SCD are good: in one pedigree followed for a mean of 8.8 years there was no graft rejection and no disease recurrence. Deep anterior lamellar keratoplasty is an alternative that preserves the (unaffected) host endothelium.

evidence.snippet: Preoperatively, BCVA ranged from logarithm of the minimum angle of resolution (logMAR) 1.7 to logMAR 0.22; yet, it was found that BCVA had improved to logMAR 0.02 at 3 years postoperatively.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies restoration of visual acuity after replacing the opacified cornea.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Replaces the opacified cornea with clear donor tissue, restoring the optical pathway without addressing the causal UBIAD1 defect.

evidence.snippet: Although de novo occurrence of mutations in UBIAD1 is extremely rare, SCD should be considered in the differential diagnosis of bilateral corneal haze and/or crystal deposition, especially in children.
evidence.explanation: Supports genetic evaluation in children and in apparently sporadic presentations.

evidence.snippet: This highlights the value of genetic testing in clinical diagnostic settings, even in the absence of a positive family history.
evidence.explanation: Direct endorsement of genetic testing regardless of family history.

treatments/2.description: Autosomal dominant transmission with a 50% offspring risk, high but age-dependent penetrance, and variable expressivity make counseling important. Because UBIAD1 has only two coding exons, targeted Sanger sequencing resolves most cases; testing is worthwhile even without a family history given documented de novo variants, and is especially useful in children and in crystal-free patients where the clinical diagnosis is ambiguous.

evidence.snippet: These findings have important implications not only for the understanding of SCD etiology but also for the efficacy of cholesterol-lowering statin therapy, which becomes limited, in part, because of UBIAD1-mediated inhibition of reductase ERAD.
evidence.explanation: Provides the mechanistic basis for expecting limited statin efficacy where UBIAD1 inhibits reductase ERAD.

treatments/3.description: Statins are appropriately prescribed for the concurrent systemic hypercholesterolemia seen in about two-thirds of patients, but there is no evidence they alter the corneal disease, and there is a mechanistic reason to expect them not to. The SCD lesion acts by blocking degradation of HMG-CoA reductase, the very enzyme statins inhibit, so the mutant protein directly opposes the compensatory turnover that statin therapy depends on. This entry is curated to record the absence of corneal benefit, not to recommend statins for SCD.

evidence.snippet: In summary, these results demonstrate that SCD-associated mutations of UBIAD1 impair its ER-to-Golgi transportation and enhance its interaction with HMGCR.
evidence.explanation: Summary statement of the canonical mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These results establish the physiological significance of UBIAD1 in cholesterol homeostasis and indicate inhibition of HMGCR ERAD contributes to SCD pathogenesis.
evidence.explanation: In vivo endorsement of the ERAD-inhibition model as contributing to SCD pathogenesis.

hypotheses/0.description: The dominant model. SCD-associated UBIAD1 is sequestered in the ER, competes with Insig-1 for HMG-CoA reductase, and blocks its sterol-accelerated ER-associated degradation. The stabilized reductase sustains cholesterol synthesis, producing corneal sterol overaccumulation. The model is supported by concordant cell-biological, biochemical, and knock-in mouse evidence, and it explains why the disease is corneal-local and why systemic statins are not expected to correct the corneal defect.

evidence.snippet: In primary keratocytes from SCD patients, a highly increased MGP expression and presence of immature MGP forms were detected. Significantly elevated plasma concentration of inactive MGP was found in SCD patients.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates a measurably abnormal vitamin-K-dependent readout in SCD corneal cells and plasma.

evidence.snippet: However, SCD patients do not exhibit typical phenotypes associated with defects of MK-4 or VKD carboxylation.
evidence.explanation: Argues against MK-4 deficiency being sufficient to explain the SCD phenotype.

hypotheses/1.description: A competing/contributing model in which reduced UBIAD1 prenyltransferase output, i.e. loss of endogenous MK-4, is itself pathogenic for the cornea, consistent with evidence that vitamin K metabolism is active in human cornea and abnormal in SCD keratocytes. The main argument against it as the primary driver is that per-variant MK-4 activity does not correlate with SCD severity (the hotspot N102S retains most MK-4 activity), and SCD patients lack the systemic phenotypes expected from MK-4 or vitamin-K-dependent carboxylation deficiency.

evidence.snippet: However, the G186R mutation significantly affected both MK-4 biosynthesis and VKD carboxylation. Other mutations exhibit varying degrees of effects on MK-4 biosynthesis and VKD carboxylation.
evidence.explanation: Shows heterogeneous, non-severity-tracking effects of SCD variants on the MK-4 arm.

open_questions/0.rationale: Both arms are demonstrably abnormal in SCD, but they make different predictions. The HMGCR arm predicts corneal sterol accumulation and is confirmed in knock-in mice. The MK-4 arm predicts vitamin-K-dependent deficits, and SCD patients do have elevated inactive matrix Gla protein, yet they lack the systemic phenotypes of MK-4 or VKD-carboxylation deficiency, and MK-4 activity per variant does not track severity (the hotspot N102S retains most of its activity). Resolving this matters therapeutically: if the MK-4 arm contributes, vitamin K2 supplementation becomes a candidate intervention; if not, only the ERAD axis is worth targeting.

evidence.snippet: The Ubiad1N100S mouse provides a promising animal model of SCD revealing that mitochondrial dysfunction is a prominent component of the disease. The different phenotype in human and mouse may due to difference in cholesterol metabolism between species.
evidence.explanation: States the mismatch and the authors' species-difference explanation.

open_questions/1.rationale: The N100S mouse models the human N102S hotspot yet shows mitochondrial abnormality and altered glycerophosphoglycerols rather than cholesterol excess, while the G184R knock-in line does accumulate corneal free cholesterol. Species differences in cholesterol metabolism are the authors' proposed explanation, but the discrepancy is unresolved and matters for choosing a preclinical model: a therapeutic candidate that normalizes cholesterol would show no benefit in the N100S line regardless of whether it works in humans.
